title: News Words: Illusion
summary: 通过博物馆中的视觉错觉理解 illusion 的含义与用法。
text: SummaryThis VOA vocabulary note introduces illusion through the Miami Paradox Museum. An illusion appears real even though it is not; an optical illusion makes the eyes perceive something differently from reality. Watch on YouTube Content 以下为原笔记中的视频转录与学习内容，保留原素材的叙述语境。 A museum in Miami, Florida specializes in works of art that stretch the imagination. ILLUSION The Miami Paradox Museum is one of several paradox museums across the world. More than 70 of its displays produce optical illusions worthy of a photograph The museum explains the math and science behind each illusion. An illusion is anything that is false or not real but that seems to be true or real. An optical illusion tricks your eyes to make you think you see something that is not present or that looks different in reality. 整理自 English / VOA / News Words: illusion。本页于 2026-09-28 整理发布。

title: Why Education is Destroying East Asia
summary: 讨论东亚教育竞争、学历扩张与毕业生就业的社会影响。
text: SummaryThis video argues that intense educational competition can create social costs when qualifications grow faster than suitable opportunities. The notes explore exam pressure, expectations, graduate employment, and the idea of elite overproduction, with vocabulary analysis and a Chinese translation. Watch on YouTube Content 以下为原笔记中的视频转录与学习内容，保留原素材的叙述语境。 Every year, on the 2nd Thursday of November, South Korea shuts down the country for an exam. 140 flights are grounded. Construction sites are ordered to stop working. And thousands of police officers are deployed to the streets to combat the mass hysteria. Inside schools across the country, thousands of teenagers are sitting an exam which will quite literally determine the outcomes of their lives. It decides what university they go to, and therefore what job they can get, their status in society, and who they can marry. It all comes down to this one moment. South Korea is one of the most educated societies in the world. And yet it’s this education that is starting to tear the country apart. This is a nation where cram schools run every day until midnight. Math tutors get paid more than star footballers. But most importantly, it’s one where society is running out of young people. South Korea has one of the lowest birth rates on the planet. And in 2024, each woman had just 0.72 children. But this phenomenon isn’t unique to South Korea. Taiwan, China, Japan — many countries across Asia consistently rank as some of the highest educationally performing countries in the world, and all ones with some of the lowest birth rates on the planet. For a time, education was seen as a kind of magic bullet, a surefire way to lift your country out of poverty. But what about when it goes a step too far? What about if there comes a point where education can start doing more harm than good? This video isn’t just about East Asia. They are just the canary in the coal mine for the rest of the Western world. This is how education is destroying East Asia, and what can be done to fix it. To understand how these countries became so consumed by education, you need to go back to 1977, in the central leadership compound in Beijing. Chairman Mao had just died, and his successor Deng Xiaoping was faced with a difficult situation, needing to massively modernize and improve the lives of over a billion people who had just gone through a series of detrimental economic policies, both under the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution. So that year, Deng decided to bring back the Gaokao. This was China’s National University Entrance Exam, but it had been banned for 11 years under Mao. The exam was a one-shot standardized test which would determine your entire future. And in that year alone, around 5.7 million candidates, from 16 all the way to as old as 40, sat down to be in with a chance of altering their future. Only 5.4% of candidates passed. But those students of the 1977 cohort have gone on to become pillars of China’s economy — across politics, technology, science, pretty much every field worth being in. Even their former premier was a student of this exam. This specific exam is a modern invention, but the roots of the idea are buried much deeper in the country’s history. Back in 605 AD, the Sui dynasty created the Keju, an exam system that — at least in theory — let any man in the empire test his way into the imperial bureaucracy, regardless of his birth status. This set a precedent which has continued in one form or another ever since. And layer onto this strong values shaped by Confucian principles, with a high emphasis placed on education as the primary vehicle for social mobility, family honor, and success. And you can see where this goes. In fact, Chinese poets nearly a thousand years ago were writing texts like this, which contained lines saying: “All pursuits are lowly, only studying is noble; a peasant at dawn, a guest at the throne by night.” So for well over a thousand years, people have been told a version of reality where studying is the only path to provide success and dignity for your family. At the time, in 1977, reintroducing this exam looked like anything but an issue. And China repeated it the next year, and the year after that. And this model was later copied by South Korea with the Suneung, and Japan with the National Center Test for University Admissions. At its core, the basic idea worked: forcing everyone, regardless of background, to compete in the same test, and therefore only selecting the brightest and best to occupy your highest positions. It was meritocracy on a scale which had never been done before. And realizing the importance that these exams could have on their children’s lives, more and more focus began to shift onto performing well in these tests. Across many Asian nations, spending on education since the 1970s has more than doubled, and whole sectors in many economies have popped up around these tests and exams. Now, education in itself clearly isn’t a bad thing — in fact, it’s quite the opposite. If you were to plot years of schooling against GDP on a graph, you can see that the correlation is overwhelming, and more education has meant richer, healthier, and more mobile societies. East Asia is also living proof of this. In a single generation, it turned war-flattened farming economies into some of the wealthiest on Earth. However, there does reach a point where it can start to do more bad than good. This is the Chilseo, which in English roughly translates to “the 7-year-old exam.” It’s a hyper-competitive test taken by six-to-seven-year-olds in order to gain access to a hagwon — Korea’s infamous elite cram school. So to be clear, this is an exam to gain entry to a school which will then help you to study more in order to pass another exam. However, if you’re only starting to consider your child’s educational future at the age of six, then you may have already left it too late. Instead, Korea’s most “caring” parents have already started preparing them for the country’s cut-throat education system — hence leading to the emergence of the even earlier “4-year-old exam” for parents who really want the best for their children. Nearly 50% of South Korean children under the age of six are now enrolled in these private cram schools, with one in four toddlers under the age of two already attending a hagwon. And this is something which not only makes parents stressed — it also makes the life of a child or teenager completely miserable. However, with all of this, it’s also led to the emergence of a new career. In 2022, job posts for a new kind of profession started to pop up around wealthier areas of Seoul. Mothers and fathers were looking for people to sit next to their children whilst they studied well into the night, to make sure they didn’t fall asleep — paying as much as $2.50 an hour. In fact, in some of Seoul’s most prestigious neighborhoods, like southern Gangnam, a few blocks can contain over 950 hagwons. And real estate prices in this small area run at 300% of comparable areas in the city. Parents, in effect, are paying specifically to live near these tutors. And the buildings themselves are something from a sci-fi film — small, soulless facilities with room after room divided by thin walls, lit by long fluorescent bulbs, even fitted with dedicated “scream pods” where students, frustrated after spending 13 hours a day studying, can go and let off steam by yelling into the abyss. Now, you might be wondering why any rational and normal parent would want to put their kid through this. However, the strange thing about this is that this is the rational move. Because university admission is positional — your kid isn’t graded against a standard, they’re graded against every other kid. And any spending by one family forces spending by all the others just to stay in place. Sure, every parent individually would be better off if everyone else stopped, but for any individual parent who stops, they sacrifice their own child. So the rational move for each individual family produces a ruinous outcome for everyone else. This is what economists call an arms race. And it’s a force so powerful that it’s become nearly impossible to stop. Back in the 1980s, South Korea’s leader was a guy named Chun Doo-hwan, and he was pretty much a dictator — so not exactly someone who’s short on power. And back then, he could see the damage that these hagwons were already starting to cause. So he decided to outright ban private tutoring. However, even the will of a dictator wasn’t enough to stop it. Instead of disappearing, it simply went underground. Tutors disguised themselves as housekeepers, lessons went on in cars, and parents risked criminal penalties, all to make their kids continue studying. Now, these hagwons are filled with enough material for an entire separate video. But the main takeaway here is that they not only make having children depressing, they have also made it extremely expensive. The UAE Population Research Institute calculates that Korea ranks the highest in the world for the cost of raising a child. The number is roughly $275,000 up to the age of 18, or roughly 7.8 times the country’s GDP per capita. In the US, by comparison, it’s 4.1 times — about a third of that. And of the Korean cost, a large share goes to a single industry: hagwons. But this cost alone doesn’t explain a birth rate of 0.72. Plenty of countries are expensive places to raise children. What makes Korea and many other places in Asia different is what kind of cost this is. It’s an arms race. A child is more like a campaign than a cost item on a spreadsheet. And in a place like Korea, a campaign can’t be half-assed. If you want your kid to succeed, it becomes all or nothing. And the maths gives a brutally clear answer: one child done properly beats two done cheaply. This maps in the data. Also, Korea’s birth rate isn’t collapsing because Koreans have stopped becoming parents, but because almost nobody goes back for a second child. By the end of the century, South Korea’s population is projected to have more than halved — collapsing from around 52 million today to just 22 million by 2100. And their population pyramid would end up looking something like this: massively top-heavy, dominated by people in their 60s and 70s, making life for the dwindling number of young people left to support them a bit of a nightmare. Okay, so remember that exam that we mentioned earlier, the Gaokao? This was the standardized test introduced by Deng Xiaoping, which in theory opened the door to anyone in the country to have the opportunity to better their life. It was perhaps the ultimate expression of meritocracy. However, there is just one issue with this: the system which has developed from it has pretty much eroded its original main advantage — improving social mobility. And the answer has to do with two self-reinforcing loops running at the same time, which make the system get worse and worse with each passing year. The first is that, rather than leveling the playing field, the existing system only serves to further reinforce its inequalities. One study found that among South Korea’s richest students, 36% make it into the top universities, whilst among the poorest, that figure is just 9%. And in Korea — much like in China, Japan, or even Taiwan — the university that you go to really matters. This is the College Scholastic Ability Test, also known as the Suneung, and it’s a brutal 10-hour-long South Korean exam which effectively goes on to determine the rest of your life. And if you’re serious about you — or your child — making it in Korea, then you’ll want them to go to one of these three universities. Collectively, they’re known as SKY, and they basically serve as the gateway into the country’s political and corporate elite. Despite only around 2% of South Korean students ever getting into these universities, that 2% goes on to fill nearly half of the country’s top CEO positions, nearly half of its senior government roles, and the vast majority of its senior judiciary. Because the stakes are so high, rich families can pay for people like this: Hyun Woo-jin. He’s a Stanford-trained math tutor who graduated from this elite school in just 3 years. However, what really makes him special is that in 2024 he was reported to earn around $15 million a year — making him richer than most of the country’s top athletes. And it’s all because he is considered the best in the country at prepping kids for this specific exam. Inside that exam, the most consequential questions are the ones called “killers.” These are deliberately designed to fall outside the public school curriculum, and they exist to separate the top 1% from everyone else. They are notoriously tough to predict. So people borrow Hyun Woo-jin’s judgment, and access to some of his programs is seen as the best way to prepare your child for the test. However, what this all means is that over three-quarters of students at SKY law schools come from high-income families. In fact, the country’s top-income households spend nearly seven times more on private tutoring than the poorest. As one researcher put it, elite universities function less like a ladder and more like a glass floor — protecting the already privileged, rather than lifting anyone up. And this happens across the continent. In China, urban students are five times more likely to be admitted to top-tier universities than rural students. Okay, so let’s say, for the sake of it, that your child managed — after battling the system and studying pretty much non-stop since they were three — to get into one of these schools. Now, in theory, they should be set — right? Well, not quite. And this is where the second cycle comes into play, and it’s potentially even more damaging than the first. In China, the phrase “neijuan” (内卷) has become one of the most popular across the nation. The two words together simply translate to “involution.” And yet their meaning has come to define the feelings of China’s youth — the realization that everyone is working harder for the same fixed reward. Back in 2022, a young creator from eastern China posted a vlog showing her normal day. And her routine went like this: after waking up around noon, she stays in bed doom-scrolling on her phone until 3:00 p.m. She then slowly migrates from bed to sofa, not bothered to go outside. She orders delivery for all three meals. She works remotely for an e-commerce company, so technically she’s not unemployed at all. Instead, she just plays life on ultra-low-power-saving mode. She basically avoids all unnecessary communication with co-workers and anyone else, for that matter. When work is done, she crawls back under the covers by 8:00 p.m., and spends the rest of the night napping and scrolling, and then the cycle repeats again. Remember, this person isn’t unemployed either, but she has pretty much given up on life. And believe it or not, this is actually a product of education, or at least of over-education, of a society. Back in 2010, Peter Turchin caused a stir by suggesting that societies collapse for a surprisingly consistent reason: they train more elites than they have room for. And he calls this particular effect “elite overproduction.” The idea itself is simple: every society only has so many genuinely elite positions. And when the number of people qualified for those positions grows faster than the positions themselves, it’s not that more and more people become elites — instead, you get a growing pool of capable, qualified people with just nowhere to put them. And China, as well as other Asian nations, have built that surplus at a scale the world has never seen. In 2026, a record 12.7 million students graduated from Chinese universities — 500,000 more than the year before, which was also a record. The issue is that there’s simply nowhere to put them. So, statistics coming from China should always be taken with a little pinch of salt — but this one, around youth employment, is particularly interesting. A few years ago, youth unemployment for 16-to-24-year-olds was hovering at around 20 to 21%. But then, in August 2023, they just stopped publishing the youth unemployment figures altogether. The interesting thing here is that, on the whole, China’s unemployment rate isn’t really an issue. Unemployment for 25-to-29-year-olds sits at around 7.2%, and for 30-to-60-year-olds it’s just 4.1%. Which tells you what you need to know about the wider economy — it isn’t broken at all. The problem is a bottleneck exactly where graduates are. So where do all of these people actually go? Education is now so deeply rooted in Chinese and East Asian Confucian morals that people aren’t simply going to stop going to university, even if they know deep down it can’t really provide for them. Instead, they just do whatever they can. More than a fifth of delivery drivers working on Meituan and Ele.me — China’s two largest platforms — now hold a university degree, and at least 70,000 of these delivery drivers have a master’s. However, a lot of people are now simply not working at all. If we go back to this word here — this was just the first in the chain. In 2021, the new word was “tangping” (躺平), “to lie flat.” Then in 2022, it changed again to “bailan” (摆烂), “let it rot.” This is the darker sequence which is developing — from diagnosis, to opting out, to now nihilism. But of all the phrases China’s youth reached for, the one that cuts deepest wasn’t new at all — it was over a hundred years old. In 2023, thousands of young graduates across the country started identifying with a more unique cultural icon: Kong Yiji, a character from a 1919 short story by Lu Xun. Kong Yiji is a failed scholar. He studied the classics, sat the imperial exams, but never passed. But he spent so long as a man of academia that it became his identity, and he couldn’t bring himself to do manual work — it would be beneath him. So he keeps wearing his scholar’s gown, the mark of an educated man, even as he slides further and further into poverty. Too learned to labor, too poor to be a scholar, he dies destitute — in the gown. And more than a century later, millions of Chinese graduates looked at their own degrees and saw the same garment: educated for jobs that don’t exist, and too invested to take the ones that do. Remember the poem from the start of this video — the one written nearly a thousand years ago: “All pursuits are lowly, only studying is noble.” For a thousand years, that was the promise: study, and you rise; study, and you earn dignity. It built the exams, the hagwons, the whole machine. Kong Yiji is what happens when the promise breaks — but the belief doesn’t. Millions more Chinese students have, and will keep, going to university, even if it serves them no benefit, simply to keep their families proud. They would rather starve as a scholar than eat as anything else. The interesting thing about Turchin’s work on elite overproduction, back in 2010, is that he wasn’t writing about China at all — sure, it checks out, but his analysis was meant for America, and the 2020s that lay ahead. And this pattern pops up everywhere in the West. In places like the UK, the number of people graduating with undergraduate degrees has skyrocketed — not necessarily because the economy needs more people with degrees, but because people have been fed this lie that all that stands between them and a successful life is a bachelor’s degree. And it’s the reason that protests are happening in India right now. At its core, it’s really just basic economics of supply and demand. The demand for graduates has more or less stayed the same, whilst the supply has exploded — which pushes the price, or the premium, of your graduate degree further down and down and down, which is exactly the machine you’ve just watched running in East Asia. The same growing pile of qualified people with nowhere to go. For years, Asia’s obsession with education has been linked to stereotypes. And it’s been easy to tell ourselves in the West a comforting story — that this was something just culturally different about Asia, something specific about Confucian philosophy, or even “tiger parenting.” However, this is not a Korean problem, or even a Chinese problem. It’s really just supply and demand — a cautionary tale running just a few years ahead of the West. 词汇与表达分析开篇场景类 shut down the country — 让整个国家停摆（不是”关闭国家”这种字面翻译，而是全国进入停摆状态） grounded (of flights) — demand — 供需关系 premium (of a degree) — 溢价，此处指学历带来的附加价值/回报 tiger parenting — “虎妈式”育儿，形容极端严苛的教育方式 cautionary tale — 警示故事 地道中文翻译每年11月的第二个星期四，韩国举国停摆，只为了一场考试：140架航班停飞，建筑工地停工，数以千计的警察被派往街头维持秩序、平息全国性的集体焦虑。 这一天，全国各地学校里，成千上万的青少年正在参加一场几乎能决定他们一生命运的考试——它决定了你能上什么大学，进而决定你能找什么工作、在社会上处于什么地位、能和什么样的人结婚。一切，都压在这一刻。 韩国是世界上教育程度最高的国家之一，可正是这种教育，正在把这个国家撕裂。这里的补习班天天开到深夜，数学家教的收入超过明星球员——但最要命的是，这个国家正在”用完”它的年轻人。 韩国的生育率是全世界最低的国家之一，2024年，平均每名女性只生0.72个孩子。而这并非韩国独有的现象：台湾、中国大陆、日本——亚洲多个国家和地区一直位居全球教育水平排行榜前列，同时也是全球生育率最低的地区之一。 曾几何时，教育被视为一种”灵丹妙药”，是国家脱贫的必胜法宝。但如果教育走过了头呢？如果教育本身开始弊大于利呢？ 这期视频讲的不只是东亚。东亚只是整个西方世界的”矿井里的金丝雀”——提前发出的预警信号。这就是教育如何一步步摧毁东亚社会，以及该如何应对。 要理解这些国家为何如此痴迷于教育，得把时间拨回1977年的北京中南海。毛主席刚刚去世，接班人邓小平面临一个艰巨的局面：如何让刚经历过”大跃进”和”文化大革命”等一系列破坏性经济政策的十几亿人过上更好的生活、实现国家现代化。 那一年，邓小平恢复了高考。这是中国的全国大学入学考试，此前在毛泽东时代已被废止长达11年。这场考试是”一考定终身”式的标准化考试，将决定一个人的整个未来。仅那一年，就有约570万从16岁到40岁不等的考生走进考场，赌上自己改变命运的机会。最终录取率只有5.4%。但那批1977级的考生后来成为中国经济各领域的中流砥柱——政界、科技界、学术界，几乎所有值得从事的领域都有他们的身影，甚至前总理也出自这批考生。 高考本身是现代产物，但这种理念的根源要追溯到更久远的历史。早在公元605年，隋朝就创立了科举制度——至少在理论上，帝国内任何男性，无论出身如何，都可以凭考试进入官僚体系。这开创了一个先例，并以各种形式延续至今。 再叠加上儒家思想塑造的价值观——把教育视为实现阶层跃迁、光耀门楣、追求成功的首要途径——事情的走向也就不难想见了。事实上，早在近千年前，中国的诗人就写下了”万般皆下品，惟有读书高””朝为田舍郎，暮登天子堂”这样的诗句。 于是，一千多年来，人们始终被灌输这样一种现实：读书是为家庭赢得成功与尊严的唯一途径。 1977年恢复高考之时，这看起来完全不成问题。此后中国年年沿用这一制度。这一模式后来也被韩国的”修能”考试、日本的”大学入学考试中心考试”所效仿。 从本质上说，这套制度的基本逻辑是有效的：让所有人无论出身，都参加同一场考试，从而只筛选出最优秀的人去占据社会最高的位置。这是史无前例、规模空前的”精英选拔制”。而当人们意识到这些考试对孩子人生的决定性影响后，社会的注意力便越来越多地转向了”如何在考试中胜出”这件事上。 自上世纪70年代以来，亚洲多国的教育支出翻了不止一番，围绕这些考试还衍生出了整条产业链。 当然，教育本身绝对不是坏事——恰恰相反。如果把受教育年限和GDP画在同一张图上，你会发现两者的相关性极其显著：更多的教育，意味着社会更富裕、更健康、阶层流动性更强。东亚正是活生生的例子：仅仅一代人的时间，就把战后一片荒芜的农业经济，变成了全球最富裕的经济体之一。 然而，凡事总有一个转折点，教育也会开始弊大于利。这就是韩国的”七岁考”——一场专为六七岁孩子设计的超高竞争考试，为的是能进入韩国声名狼藉的精英补习班”学院”（hagwon）。 说白了，这是一场”考补习班”的考试——而进补习班，是为了以后能更好地准备下一场考试。可如果你到孩子六岁才开始为他的教育前途操心，可能已经太晚了。于是韩国那些”最上心”的父母早已提前布局，由此还催生出了更早的”四岁考”，专为那些一心想给孩子最好条件的家长而设。 如今，韩国近一半六岁以下的儿童已经被送进这类私立补习班，四分之一两岁以下的幼儿已经在上”学院”了。这不仅让家长倍感压力，也让孩子和青少年的生活变得苦不堪言。 不过，这一切也催生出了一种新职业。2022年，首尔富裕地区开始出现一种新的招聘广告：父母想雇人陪自己的孩子挑灯夜读，只为确保孩子不会打瞌睡——时薪高达2.5美元。 事实上，在首尔一些最”高档”的社区，比如江南区南部，短短几个街区内就聚集了950多家补习班。这片区域的房价高达周边同类地区的三倍——家长们花大价钱，就是为了住得离这些补习班近一点。 而这些补习班的建筑本身，仿佛出自科幻电影：一间间用薄墙隔开、毫无生气的小房间，头顶是长长的荧光灯管，甚至还配有专门的”尖叫舱”——供每天学习13个小时后濒临崩溃的学生，进去朝深渊大喊发泄情绪。 你可能会想，哪个理智正常的父母会愿意让孩子经历这些？但奇怪的是，这恰恰是”理性”的选择。因为大学录取本质上是”位次竞争”——你的孩子不是和某个客观标准比，而是和其他所有孩子比。只要有一家在加码，就会倒逼所有人跟着加码，才能维持原地不掉队。当然，如果大家都停下来，每个家庭个体上都会更好过；但只要有一个家庭率先停下，牺牲的就是自家孩子的前途。于是，每个家庭个体上的”理性选择”，最终酿成了对所有人都灾难性的集体结果。经济学家称之为”军备竞赛”——一种一旦启动就几乎无法叫停的强大力量。 早在上世纪80年代，韩国领导人全斗焕——一个不折不扣的独裁者，手中权力可谓无人能及——就已经看到了这些补习班带来的危害，于是下令全面禁止私人补习。然而，即便是独裁者的意志，也没能真正遏制住它。补习并未消失，只是转入了地下：家教伪装成保姆，课程在车里偷偷进行，家长甘冒被追究刑责的风险，只为让孩子继续读书。 这些补习班的故事本身足够拍一整期视频，但这里的核心结论是：它们不仅让生养孩子变成一件令人沮丧的事，更让它变得极其昂贵。阿联酋人口研究所计算显示，韩国养育一个孩子的成本全球最高——到18岁为止，大约需要27.5万美元，相当于该国人均GDP的7.8倍；相比之下，美国这一比例是4.1倍，约为韩国的三分之一。而在韩国这笔支出中，很大一部分都流向了同一个行业——补习班。 但光是成本高，并不能完全解释0.72的生育率。世界上有很多国家养孩子都很贵。真正让韩国和亚洲其他一些地方与众不同的，是这笔成本的”性质”：这是一场军备竞赛。养一个孩子更像是一场”战役”，而不是账本上的一项支出。而在韩国这样的地方，这场战役容不得半点敷衍。如果你想让孩子出人头地，那就是全力以赴，没有中间地带。数学给出的答案冷酷而清晰：与其马马虎虎养两个，不如全力以赴养一个。 数据也印证了这一点：韩国生育率的崩塌，并非因为韩国人不再愿意为人父母，而是因为几乎没有人愿意生第二个孩子。 到本世纪末，韩国人口预计将萎缩超过一半——从如今的约5200万，跌至2100年的约2200万。届时该国的人口金字塔将变得极度”头重脚轻”，由六七十岁的老年人主导，而所剩无几的年轻人，则要扛起赡养他们的重担，处境堪忧。 好了，还记得我们前面提到的”高考”吗？这本是邓小平推行的标准化考试，理论上向全国每一个人敞开了改善人生的大门，堪称精英选拔制度的极致体现。然而问题就出在这里：这套制度发展至今，已经在很大程度上侵蚀了它最初的核心优势——促进社会流动。而背后的原因，在于两个同时运转、相互强化的恶性循环，使这套系统一年比一年更加糟糕。 第一个循环是：这套制度非但没有拉平竞争的起跑线，反而在不断强化原有的不平等。一项研究发现，在韩国最富裕的学生中，有36%能考入顶尖大学；而在最贫困的学生中，这一比例仅为9%。 在韩国——正如在中国、日本乃至台湾一样——你上的是哪所大学，真的至关重要。所谓”大学修学能力考试”（修能），是一场长达10小时、堪称残酷的韩国考试，其结果实际上将决定你此后的整个人生。如果你——或你的孩子——想在韩国真正出人头地，那你会希望进入这三所大学，它们合称”SKY”，基本上是通往这个国家政界与商界精英圈层的唯一入口。 尽管每年只有约2%的韩国学生能考入这三所大学，但正是这2%的人，占据了全国近一半的顶级CEO职位、近一半的高级政府职务，以及绝大多数的高级司法职位。 正因为赌注如此之高，富裕家庭愿意为像玄佑镇这样的人一掷千金——他是一位斯坦福出身、只用三年就从这所名校毕业的数学名师。而真正让他与众不同的是，据报道，他在2024年的年收入高达约1500万美元，比该国大多数顶尖运动员赚得还多。而这一切，只因为他被公认为全国最擅长辅导学生应对这场特定考试的人。 在这场考试中，最关键的题目被称为”杀手题”——这些题目被刻意设计得超出公立学校教学大纲的范围，目的就是把最顶尖的1%和其他所有人区分开来。这类题目出了名地难以预测，因此人们纷纷借重玄佑镇的判断力，能接触到他部分课程，也被视为备考这场考试的最佳途径。 然而，这一切意味着，SKY法学院里超过四分之三的学生都来自高收入家庭。事实上，该国收入最高的家庭在私人补习上的花费，几乎是最贫困家庭的七倍。 正如一位研究者所说：精英大学与其说是一架”向上流动的阶梯”，不如说是一块”玻璃地板”——它保护的是本已占据优势的人，而不是把任何人往上托举。而这种现象在整个亚洲大陆都普遍存在：在中国，城市学生进入顶尖大学的概率是农村学生的五倍。 好，那我们姑且假设，你的孩子从三岁起就一路搏杀、几乎不间断地学习，终于成功考入了这些名校之一。理论上，从此就万事大吉了，对吧？——并不尽然。这正是第二个恶性循环登场的地方，而它带来的伤害，可能比第一个还要更深。 在中国，”内卷”这个词已经成为全国最流行的说法之一。这两个字翻译成英文就是”involution”，但它所承载的含义，早已成为中国年轻一代情绪的真实写照——人人都在更拼命地努力，换来的却是同一份原地踏步的固定回报。 2022年，中国东部一位年轻的创作者发布了一条记录自己日常的视频。她的一天是这样度过的：中午起床后，在床上刷手机刷到下午三点；接着从床上慢慢挪到沙发上，懒得出门；一日三餐全靠外卖解决；她其实为一家电商公司远程工作，所以严格来说并没有失业——她只是把生活调成了”超低功耗省电模式”：尽量避免和同事乃至任何人产生不必要的交流。等工作结束，她晚上八点就爬回被窝，剩下的时间不是打盹就是刷手机，第二天照此循环。请注意，这个人也并非失业，但她几乎已经对生活彻底放弃了希望。 而信不信由你，这其实正是”教育”、或者更准确地说，是一个社会”教育过剩”的产物。早在2010年，彼得·图尔钦（Peter Turchin）就曾提出一个引发轩然大波的观点：社会崩溃往往有一个惊人一致的原因——社会培养出的精英数量，超过了它所能容纳的精英岗位数量。他把这种现象称为”精英生产过剩”。 这个道理其实很简单：任何一个社会，真正意义上的”精英职位”数量都是有限的。当具备相应资质的人数增长速度超过职位数量的增长速度时，结果并不是有更多人真的成为了精英，而是出现了一大批有能力、有资质，却无处安放的人。 而中国以及其他亚洲国家，正在以史无前例的规模累积这样的”过剩人群”。2026年，中国高校毕业生人数达到创纪录的1270万，比上一年（同样是历史最高纪录）还多出50万。问题在于，根本没有足够多的位置来安置他们。 关于中国的统计数据，向来需要打点折扣看待，但有一个和青年就业相关的数字格外值得玩味：几年前，16至24岁人群的青年失业率一度徘徊在20%到21%左右。可到了2023年8月，官方干脆彻底停止公布这一数据。 耐人寻味的是，从整体来看，中国的失业率其实并不是什么大问题：25至29岁人群的失业率约为7.2%，30至60岁人群仅为4.1%——这说明整体经济其实运转良好，并没有出什么大问题。问题恰恰卡在应届毕业生这个环节上，是一个结构性的”瓶颈”。 那么，这些人到底都去哪儿了？教育理念在中国乃至整个东亚的儒家伦理中根植太深，以至于即便人们心里清楚上大学未必能带来实际回报，也不会真的停止追逐大学文凭。于是，他们只能尽力去找任何能做的事：在美团和饿了么这两大中国最大外卖平台上，超过五分之一的骑手拥有大学学历，其中至少7万人拥有硕士学位。 然而，也有相当一部分人，干脆彻底选择了”不工作”。如果我们回顾一下前面提到的这个词——它只是这条演变链条中的第一环。2021年，网络流行语是”躺平”；到2022年，又演变成了”摆烂”。这是一条越来越黑暗的演变轨迹：从”自我诊断问题”，到”主动退出竞争”，再到如今的”彻底虚无主义”。 但在中国年轻人所借用的所有说法中，最扎心的那一个，其实一点也不新——它已经有一百多年历史了。2023年，成千上万的应届毕业生开始将自己代入一个更加独特的文化形象：孔乙己——鲁迅1919年短篇小说中的人物。 孔乙己是一个屡试不第的读书人：他熟读经典、参加科举，却始终未能考中。但他花了太久时间沉浸在”读书人”这个身份里，以至于这已经成了他的自我认同，让他放不下架子去从事体力劳动——那在他看来是有失身份的事。于是他始终穿着那件象征读书人身份的长衫，即便自己的生活每况愈下，也不愿脱下。”高不成低不就”，最终，他穿着那件长衫，穷困潦倒地死去。 一百多年后，无数中国大学毕业生看着自己手中的文凭，看到的却是同一件”长衫”：为一些根本不存在的工作而受教育，却又因为投入太多而不甘心去做那些真正存在的工作。 还记得这期视频开头引用的那句诗吗？——那首近千年前写下的诗句：”万般皆下品，惟有读书高。”一千年来，这一直是社会给出的承诺：读书，你就能向上流动；读书，你就能赢得尊严。正是这个承诺，建起了科举、建起了补习班、建起了这整台”教育机器”。而”孔乙己文学”的出现，恰恰是这个承诺破碎之后的产物——可即便承诺已经破碎，人们的信念却并未随之消失。仍会有千千万万的中国学生继续走进大学，即便这对他们自己毫无实际益处，仅仅是为了不让家人失望。他们宁愿”穷酸地当读书人”，也不愿”随便找份活儿糊口”。 有意思的是，图尔钦2010年那篇关于”精英生产过剩”的研究，压根不是在讨论中国——虽然套用在中国身上确实成立，但他分析的对象其实是美国，以及接下来即将到来的21世纪20年代。而这种模式，如今正在整个西方世界不断重演。以英国为例，拿到本科学位的人数正在飞速攀升——这并非因为经济真的需要这么多有学位的人，而是因为人们被灌输了这样一个”谎言”：一张本科文凭，就是自己与成功人生之间唯一的距离。这也正是眼下印度爆发抗议活动的原因之一。 归根结底，这不过是最基本的供需经济学：对毕业生的需求大体保持不变，而毕业生的供给却在急剧膨胀——这必然会不断压低一张大学文凭所能带来的”溢价”，一路走低、走低、再走低。而这，正是你刚刚在东亚亲眼见证的那台机器的运转逻辑：同样是一大批有资质、却无处可去的人。 多年来，人们习惯把亚洲对教育的这种痴迷，归结为某种”文化特殊性”的刻板印象。在西方，我们也乐于用一个自我安慰的说法来解释它——认为这只是亚洲在文化上的”特殊之处”，是儒家哲学的产物，或者干脆归咎于所谓的”虎妈式教育”。然而，这根本不是韩国的问题，甚至也不只是中国的问题。归根结底，这不过是供需关系使然——一个只是比西方提前上演了几年的警世故事罢了。 整理自 English / Journal / 003。本页于 2026-09-28 整理发布。

title: Learn How to Think In English ( Stop Translating in Your Head )
summary: 通过五种日常练习逐渐用英语思考，减少逐字翻译。
text: SummaryThis lesson offers five daily exercises for thinking in English: naming nearby objects, talking to yourself, connecting words with images, repeating easy audio, and spending small moments of the day in English. The notes emphasize regular, simple practice and include vocabulary and a Chinese translation. Watch on YouTube Content 以下为原笔记中的视频转录与学习内容，保留原素材的叙述语境。 In this video, I will show you five simple daily exercises that can slowly help you improve your English naturally. These exercises are easy to follow. They do not require perfect grammar, and if you practice them every day, you will slowly notice that English starts coming into your mind more automatically. So stay with me until the end, because the last exercise is simple, powerful, and something most learners never try. Let’s begin with the first exercise. Exercise number one is called “Name Everything Around You.” Right now, look around your room and notice the things near you — maybe you see a phone, a chair, a bottle, a fan, a window, or a bag. Now say those words directly in English, without translating them in your head. After that, start making small natural sentences. You can say things like “My phone is on the table” or “The window is open today.” The goal is not to speak perfect English — the goal is to make your brain react to real objects using English immediately. You can also do this outside while walking — look at the road, the trees, the cars, the shops, and describe them in simple English. At first, your brain may still try to translate everything, and that is completely normal, but if you continue doing this every day, your brain slowly becomes faster at understanding English directly. Now let’s move to exercise number two. This exercise is one of the best ways to improve speaking confidence, and it is called “Talk to Yourself in English.” Yes, it may feel a little strange at first, but it works incredibly well, because there is no pressure. When you are alone, you do not feel embarrassed, you do not worry about mistakes, and because of that, your brain feels relaxed enough to practice naturally. When you wake up in the morning, try describing your actions in English. You can say “I need to get out of bed” or “I feel very sleepy today.” While making tea or coffee, you can say “The water is getting hot” or “I need some sugar.” When you are walking outside, describe what you see around you. At the beginning, your sentences may feel small and simple, and that is perfectly fine — simple English spoken daily is much more powerful than advanced English that you never use. Now let’s talk about exercise number three, which is extremely powerful for memory and fluency. This exercise is called “Use Pictures Instead of Translation.” Whenever you learn a new English word, stop connecting it to your language — instead, connect it to a picture, action, or feeling. For example, if you learn the word “hungry,” do not immediately think about the meaning in your own language — instead, imagine yourself looking at delicious food after a long day. If you learn the word “angry,” picture someone shouting with an upset face. If you learn the word “run,” imagine a person running quickly on a road. Your brain understands images much faster than translations — that is why visual learning is so powerful. So from today, whenever you learn a new word, create a small image or scene in your mind. This habit will slowly train your brain to understand English directly. Now let’s move to exercise number four. This exercise can seriously improve your speaking speed, and it is called “Listen and Repeat Immediately.” Choose easy English audio from YouTube videos, podcasts, interviews, or short movie clips. Listen carefully to one sentence, then pause the audio and repeat the sentence immediately. Try to copy the pronunciation, speed, and emotion as closely as possible. For example, if the speaker says “I don’t know what happened,” pause the video and repeat the same sentence naturally. The reason this exercise works so well is because it trains your brain to react quickly in English without spending too much time translating — you are teaching your mouth and your brain to work together automatically. But here is something very important: do not practice with content that is too difficult. Many learners watch fast movies with advanced vocabulary, understand almost nothing, and then feel disappointed. Instead, start with easy English that you can understand comfortably. Easy practice builds confidence, and confidence helps you stay consistent, and consistency is what truly changes your English over time. Now let’s talk about the final exercise, and honestly, this one can completely change the way you think in English. Exercise number five is called “Live Small Moments in English.” This exercise means choosing small parts of your day where you think only in English. For example, while brushing your teeth, try describing your actions in English. While eating food, think about the taste, smell, and texture in English. When you are outside, quietly describe the people, buildings, weather, and sounds around you. You might say things like “The sky looks beautiful today” or “That man is wearing a blue jacket.” At first, your brain may feel tired because it is learning a completely new habit, but after some time, something amazing begins to happen — you no longer need to translate every sentence before speaking, and that is the moment when your fluency truly starts growing. Many learners believe they must first master grammar or memorize thousands of words, but that mindset only delays progress. Thinking in English is not the final result of fluency — it is the path that leads to fluency. The more you practice simple English every day, the more natural the language becomes inside your mind. And your brain works exactly like a muscle: if you practice translation every day, your brain becomes faster at translating, but if you practice direct English thinking every day, your brain becomes faster at thinking in English naturally. So build the habit that actually helps you speak fluently, even if your English is simple, even if you make mistakes sometimes — keep practicing anyway, because every small sentence is helping your brain become more comfortable with English. So, starting today, practice these five exercises daily: name the things around you, talk to yourself in English, use pictures instead of translation, listen and repeat simple English audio, and finally, live small moments of your day completely in English. Do not expect instant results after one day, because language learning takes time. But if you stay consistent, one day you will suddenly notice something incredible — you answered a question in English without translating first, and that moment feels amazing, because you finally realize that English is becoming natural for you. If you enjoyed this video, write in the comments “I will think in English from today,” and also tell me which exercise you want to try first. Don’t forget to like the video, subscribe to the channel, and continue practicing your English every single day, because fluency is built slowly through small daily habits. Vocabulary & Expressions核心词汇/短语 表达 含义/用法 naturally 自然而然地；这里强调”不刻意、慢慢内化”的学习效果，跟 fluently 不同，fluently 强调”流利”，naturally 强调”不生硬” react to 对……做出反应；固定搭配，后接介词 to，”让大脑对实物做出英语反应” embarrassed 尴尬的；比 shy（害羞）更强调”因出丑而难为情” connect A to B 把A和B联系起来；这里指”把单词和画面联系起来”而非”和母语联系起来” picture / imagine 想象，在心里描绘画面；作动词用，比 think of 更具画面感 pause and repeat 暂停并跟读；语言学习中”精听跟读法”的标准说法 copy the pronunciation, speed and emotion 模仿发音、语速和情绪；模仿的三个维度，这是跟读练习的关键动作 comfortably 舒适地，轻松地；”understand comfortably” 指”能轻松听懂”，强调可理解性输入（comprehensible input）的重要性 consistency 坚持性，持续性；这是全文反复强调的核心概念，比 persistence 更中性、更常用于习惯养成语境 live small moments in English 直译”用英语过日常小片段”，是作者自创的表达，指”挑一天中的零碎时间完全用英语思考” the final result of fluency vs the path that leads to fluency 结果 vs 路径的对比句式，是英语说理文中常见的修辞手法（不是……而是……） works like a muscle 像肌肉一样运作；一个常见比喻，”用进废退”，练什么就强化什么neural pathway delay progress 延误进步；delay 作及物动词，”拖延/推迟”某事发生 语法/表达小结 全文大量使用 祈使句（Look, Say, Try, Choose, Imagine…）——这是教学类脚本的典型特征，直接给出行动指令。 条件句 if… you will… 反复出现，强调”练习-效果”的因果关系。 not A but B 句式（如 “not the final result… but the path…”）是全篇说理的核心修辞，值得重点掌握，可以套用在议论文写作里。 中文翻译在这个视频里，我会教你五个简单的日常小练习，能慢慢帮你自然地提升英语。这些练习很容易上手，不需要你掌握完美的语法。只要每天坚持练习，你会慢慢发现，英语开始更自动地涌进你的脑海。所以一定要看到最后，因为最后一个练习简单又有效，而且是大多数学习者从来没试过的。 我们先来看第一个练习——“说出你身边的一切”。现在环顾一下你的房间，注意你身边的东西——也许你看到了手机、椅子、瓶子、风扇、窗户或包。直接用英语说出这些单词，不要在脑子里先翻译。然后，开始造一些简单自然的句子，比如”My phone is on the table”（我的手机在桌子上）或者”The window is open today”（今天窗户开着）。目标不是说出完美的英语,而是让你的大脑对眼前的真实物品立刻用英语做出反应。你也可以在外面走路时这样做——看看马路、树木、车辆、商店，用简单的英语描述它们。一开始你的大脑可能还是会忍不住先翻译,这完全正常。但只要你每天坚持,你的大脑会慢慢变得更擅长直接用英语理解。 接下来是第二个练习,这是提升口语自信最好的方法之一,叫做”自言自语说英语”。没错,一开始可能会觉得有点奇怪,但效果非常好,因为这样做没有压力。一个人独处时,你不会感到尴尬,也不用担心出错,正因如此,你的大脑才能放松下来,自然地进行练习。早上醒来时,试着用英语描述自己的动作,比如说”I need to get out of bed”(我该起床了)或”I feel very sleepy today”(我今天好困)。泡茶或煮咖啡时,可以说”The water is getting hot”(水要开了)或”I need some sugar”(我需要点糖)。走在外面时,描述你看到的一切。刚开始你的句子可能又短又简单,但完全没关系——每天说简单的英语,远比你从不使用的高级英语更有力量。 再来看第三个练习,这个练习对记忆力和流利度极其有效,叫做”用画面代替翻译”。每次学一个新单词时,不要马上把它和你的母语联系起来,而是把它和一个画面、动作或感受联系起来。比如,学到”hungry”(饥饿)这个词时,不要立刻想它的中文意思,而是想象自己在漫长的一天后看到美味食物的样子。学到”angry”(生气)这个词,就想象一个人板着脸大喊大叫的画面。学到”run”(跑)这个词,就想象一个人在路上飞快奔跑的样子。大脑理解画面的速度远远快于理解翻译——这就是为什么”视觉化学习”如此有效。所以从今天起,每学一个新单词,就在脑海中构建一个小画面或小场景。这个习惯会慢慢训练你的大脑,让它直接用英语理解事物。 接下来是第四个练习,它能显著提升你的口语反应速度,叫做”即时听说跟读”。找一些简单的英语音频,可以来自YouTube视频、播客、访谈或电影片段。仔细听一句话,然后暂停音频,立刻跟着重复这句话。尽量模仿说话人的发音、语速和情绪。比如,如果说话人说的是”I don’t know what happened”(我不知道发生了什么),你就暂停视频,自然地重复这句话。这个练习之所以效果这么好,是因为它训练你的大脑快速对英语做出反应,而不用花太多时间去翻译——你是在训练嘴巴和大脑自动配合。但有一点非常重要:不要用太难的内容来练习。很多学习者一上来就看语速很快、词汇很难的电影,几乎什么都听不懂,结果感到很沮丧。相反,一定要从自己能轻松听懂的简单英语开始。简单的练习能建立信心,信心又能帮你坚持下去,而坚持,才是真正能改变你英语水平的关键。 最后来说说第五个练习,老实说,这一个可能会彻底改变你用英语思考的方式。第五个练习叫做”用英语过生活中的小片段”。也就是说,挑出一天中的某些零碎时刻,只用英语去思考。比如,刷牙的时候,试着用英语描述你的动作;吃饭的时候,用英语想一想食物的味道、气味和口感;在外面的时候,悄悄地用英语描述周围的人、建筑、天气和声音。你可以说”The sky looks beautiful today”(今天的天空真美)或者”That man is wearing a blue jacket”(那个人穿着一件蓝色夹克)。一开始,你的大脑可能会觉得有点累,因为它在学习一个全新的习惯,但过一段时间后,神奇的事情就会发生——你不再需要在开口之前先把每句话翻译一遍,而这一刻,正是你的流利度真正开始成长的时刻。 很多学习者以为必须先掌握语法,或者先背下成千上万个单词,但这种想法只会拖慢你的进步。用英语思考并不是流利的最终结果,而是通往流利的必经之路。你每天练习简单英语的次数越多,这门语言在你脑海中就会变得越自然。你的大脑运作方式,其实和肌肉一模一样:如果你每天练习的是翻译,你的大脑就会越来越擅长翻译;但如果你每天练习的是直接用英语思考,你的大脑就会越来越擅长自然地用英语思考。所以,要培养真正能帮你说好英语的习惯——哪怕你的英语还很简单,哪怕你偶尔会犯错,也要坚持练下去,因为每一个小小的句子,都在帮你的大脑变得更适应英语。 所以,从今天开始,每天练习这五个小练习:说出你身边的事物、自言自语说英语、用画面代替翻译、精听并跟读简单的英语音频,以及用英语过完一天中的零碎小片段。不要指望练一天就能立刻见效,因为语言学习需要时间。但只要你坚持下去,总有一天你会突然发现一件不可思议的事——你在没有先翻译的情况下,用英语回答了一个问题。而那一刻会让你感到无比美妙,因为你终于意识到,英语正在变得对你来说自然而然。 如果你喜欢这个视频,欢迎在评论区写下”我从今天起要用英语思考”,也告诉我你最想先尝试哪一个练习。别忘了点赞视频、订阅频道,并且每天坚持练习你的英语,因为流利,正是通过日积月累的小习惯慢慢建立起来的。 整理自 English / Journal / 002。本页于 2026-09-28 整理发布。

title: Personal Finance For Dummies - Eric Tyson (Book Summary)
summary: 从预算、债务到投资与保险，建立个人理财的基本框架。
text: SummaryThis video summarizes Eric Tyson’s Personal Finance for Dummies. The notes introduce budgeting, financial planning, banking and credit, debt, investing, insurance, and property, then examine useful financial expressions and provide a Chinese translation. Watch on YouTube Content 以下为原笔记中的视频转录与学习内容，保留原素材的叙述语境。 Welcome back to our channel, where we bring you summaries of popular books. Today, we’re diving into Personal Finance for Dummies by Eric Tyson, a comprehensive guide to managing your money and achieving financial success. Whether you’re a financial novice or looking to enhance your money management skills, this book has got you covered. So let’s get started. Chapter 1: Getting Your Financial House in OrderIn this chapter, Tyson emphasizes the importance of organizing your finances. He guides readers through creating a budget, tracking expenses, and setting financial goals. With practical tips and insights, he helps you take control of your financial life from the very beginning. Chapter 2: Planning Your Financial FutureTyson explores the concept of financial planning in this chapter. He explains how to assess your current financial situation, determine your net worth, and develop a long-term financial plan. From retirement savings to investments, he provides valuable guidance on securing your financial future. Chapter 3: Banking and CreditThis chapter delves into the world of banking and credit. Tyson offers advice on choosing the right bank, managing your checking and savings accounts, and using credit responsibly. He helps you navigate the complexities of credit scores, loans, and credit cards, ensuring that you make informed financial decisions. Chapter 4: Managing DebtDebt management is a crucial aspect of personal finance, and Tyson tackles it head-on in this chapter. He discusses strategies for reducing debt, understanding interest rates, and dealing with creditors. With his expert guidance, you’ll learn how to take control of your debt and pave the way to financial freedom. Chapter 5: Investing for the FutureInvesting can be intimidating, but Tyson simplifies the process in this chapter. He introduces various investment options such as stocks, bonds, and mutual funds. He also explains the importance of diversification and offers tips for building a successful investment portfolio tailored to your goals and risk tolerance. Chapter 6: Protecting Your WealthProtecting your hard-earned money is essential, and Tyson highlights this in Chapter 6. He covers insurance policies, including health, life, and property insurance, and provides insights on making smart insurance choices. With his guidance, you’ll learn how to safeguard your wealth and mitigate potential risks. Chapter 7: Property InvestingFor those interested in real estate, this chapter provides a comprehensive overview of property investing. Tyson explains the pros and cons of owning rental properties, navigating the housing market, and maximizing your returns. Whether you’re a beginner or considering expanding your property portfolio, this chapter offers valuable insights. And there you have it — a summary of Personal Finance for Dummies by Eric Tyson. This book covers a wide range of topics, from budgeting to investing, providing practical advice for managing your money wisely. Remember, financial literacy is a journey, and with the knowledge gained from this book, you can take control of your finances and build a brighter financial future. Thanks for watching, and don’t forget to subscribe to our channel for more book summaries and financial tips. Stay financially savvy. 动词(emphasizes/explores/discusses/highlights)…” 的固定句式来引出每章主题，这是书评/总结类视频的典型模板句型，适合仿写。 “From A to B” 结构（如 “from retirement savings to investments”，”from budgeting to investing”）常用于概括范围广泛的内容，语言精炼，值得积累。 中文翻译欢迎回到我们的频道，这里为大家带来热门书籍的精华解读。今天我们要聊的是埃里克·泰森（Eric Tyson）所著的《傻瓜理财书》（Personal Finance for Dummies），这是一本教你如何管理金钱、实现财务成功的实用指南。无论你是理财小白，还是想进一步提升理财能力，这本书都能满足你的需求。那我们马上开始吧。 第一章：理清你的财务状况在这一章中，泰森强调了梳理个人财务的重要性。他手把手教读者如何制定预算、追踪支出、设定财务目标。通过实用的建议和洞见，帮助你从一开始就掌控自己的财务生活。 第二章：规划你的财务未来泰森在本章探讨了财务规划的概念。他讲解了如何评估当前财务状况、计算净资产，以及制定长期财务计划。从退休储蓄到投资布局，他为你稳固财务未来提供了宝贵的指导。 第三章：银行与信用本章深入讲解银行与信用的相关知识。泰森就如何选择合适的银行、管理支票与储蓄账户，以及负责任地使用信用给出建议。他帮你理清信用评分、贷款和信用卡背后的复杂逻辑，确保你能做出明智的财务决策。 第四章：债务管理债务管理是个人理财中至关重要的一环，泰森在本章正面直击这一难题。他讨论了减少债务的策略、理解利率的方式，以及如何与债权人打交道。在他的专业指导下，你将学会掌控债务，迈向财务自由之路。 第五章：为未来投资投资听起来令人望而生畏，但泰森在本章把它讲得通俗易懂。他介绍了股票、债券、共同基金等多种投资方式，同时阐述了资产配置多元化的重要性，并提供了打造适合自身目标与风险承受能力的投资组合的技巧。 第六章：守护你的财富守护辛苦挣来的钱至关重要，泰森在第六章重点讲解了这一点。他涵盖了健康险、寿险、财产险等保险类型，并就如何做出明智的保险选择给出建议。在他的指导下，你将学会保护财富、降低潜在风险。 第七章：房产投资对于对房地产感兴趣的读者，本章全面概述了房产投资。泰森讲解了持有出租房产的利弊、如何应对楼市变化，以及如何实现收益最大化。无论你是新手，还是想扩大自己的房产投资组合，这一章都能带给你有价值的启发。 以上就是埃里克·泰森《傻瓜理财书》的精华总结。这本书内容涵盖广泛，从预算到投资无所不包，为你提供了切实可行的理财建议。请记住，金融素养是一场持续的旅程，凭借从这本书中获得的知识,你完全可以掌控自己的财务，开创更加光明的财务未来。感谢观看，别忘了订阅我们的频道，获取更多好书解读和理财资讯。愿你始终保持理财智慧！ 整理自 English / Journal / 🏙️ 001。本页于 title: One-on-One with Warren Buffett
summary: 巴菲特访谈中的经济、市场、不平等与慈善话题。
text: SummaryThis historical interview with Warren Buffett covers the American economy, inequality, wages, tax credits, political donations, markets, philanthropy, and the American dream. The notes are organized into eight topics, each combining interview passages, vocabulary, and Chinese translation. Watch on YouTube Content 以下为原笔记中的视频转录与学习内容，保留原素材的叙述语境。 第一段：经济现状断句后原文： “We’re seeing some recent cracks in the US economy, right? You’ve got retail and auto sales down, you’ve got forecasts for first-quarter earnings looking lower than has been expected — to fall for the first time since 2012. Is this a blip, or is this the beginning of a bigger shift?” “No, I don’t see any real weakness in the economy. Home building has been slow, and it continues slow, but the economy has been improving since the fall of 2009, and it continues to improve. So I just don’t see it. I’ve seen the February figures for our companies, and there’s parts that are a little stronger than others, but that’s been the case ever since the fall of 2009. We’ve been on an upward course, and people talk about double dips, and they talk about acceleration — in the end it just keeps moving ahead. And I think it’s quite a tribute actually to our policymakers, all the way back to the fall of 2008, that we’ve recovered like we have from what was an incredible panic.” 词汇与表达分析： 表达 含义 cracks in the economy “经济出现裂痕”——比喻经济开始显露隐患 a blip 一次短暂的、无关大局的小波动 double dip(s) “二次探底”，经济学术语，指经济复苏后再次下滑 a tribute to X 对X的一种肯定/证明（”这也证明了…的功劳”） panic (经济语境) 特指”恐慌性金融危机”，如1929年大萧条前的”the Panic of 1929” 中文翻译： “最近美国经济出现了一些裂痕，对吧？零售和汽车销售在下滑，第一季度盈利预期也被下调——这将是2012年以来盈利首次下滑。这只是一次小波动，还是更大转变的开始？” “不，我没看到经济有什么真正的疲软。住房建设一直缓慢，现在依然缓慢，但经济从2009年秋天以来一直在改善，而且还在持续改善。所以我确实没看到（衰退迹象）。我看过我们旗下公司2月份的数据，有些板块确实比其他板块强一些，但这种情况从2009年秋天起就一直存在。我们一直处于上升通道，人们总在谈论’二次探底’，谈论’加速衰退’，但最终经济总是在往前走。我认为，从2008年秋天算起，这其实要归功于我们的政策制定者——我们能从那场惊人的恐慌中恢复过来，实属不易。” 第二段：耶伦讲话与经济风险断句： “Fed Chair Janet Yellen said on Friday: if underlying conditions had truly returned to normal, the economy should be booming. Where’s the risk?” “Well, I don’t think there’s a particular risk in the economy. Over time we will have recessions from time to time, and we had a real doozy in the fall of 2008 and early 2009, and that has had more consequences than other recessions have had post–World War II. But the American economy is a wonderful machine — it really works. It’s worked since 1776, and it’ll continue to work. But we will continue to have ups and downs, because for some Americans — they listen to that and they say, ‘It’s not working for me,’ and they see stagnant wage growth and they feel like it’s getting increasingly hard to get by year by year. So who’s winning, Wall Street or Main Street?” “The extreme rich are clearly winning.” 词汇分析： 表达 含义 a real doozy 口语，”一个厉害的家伙/事件”，这里指”一场非常严重的危机” post–World War II 二战后 a wonderful machine 比喻美国经济体系是一台运转良好的机器 stagnant wage growth 工资增长停滞 get by 勉强维持生计 Wall Street vs. Main Street 华尔街(金融资本)对普通民众(实体经济/平民)的经典对照表达 翻译： “美联储主席珍妮特·耶伦周五说：如果经济基本面真的恢复正常，经济现在应该是一片繁荣。那风险在哪？” “我不认为经济存在特别的风险。从长期看，我们总会时不时经历衰退，2008年秋天到2009年初我们经历了一场真正严重的危机，它带来的后果比二战后其他任何一次衰退都更大。但美国经济是一台了不起的机器——它确实运转良好，从1776年至今一直如此，未来也会继续运转下去。但我们仍会有起有落，因为对一些美国人来说，他们听到这些话会说’这对我不管用’，他们看到工资增长停滞不前，感觉一年比一年更难维持生计。那么到底是华尔街赢了，还是普通老百姓赢了？” “显然是极端富有的那群人赢了。” 第三段：贫富差距（Forbes 400）断句： “If you look at the Forbes 400, they had an aggregate net worth of $92 billion in 1982. It’s $2.3 trillion today — 25 times as much. So the very rich have done exceptionally well in this economy. Other people have done okay on balance, but it’s certainly the super-rich — it’s really been concentrated. You can just look at that figure: from $92 billion to $2.3 trillion.” 词汇分析： 表达 含义 aggregate net worth 总净资产 have done exceptionally well 表现极为出色（这里指财富暴增） on balance 总体而言，权衡利弊后 concentrated (财富语境) 财富”集中”于少数人手中 翻译： “看看《福布斯》400富豪榜，1982年他们的总净资产是920亿美元，如今是2.3万亿美元——是原来的25倍。所以在这个经济体系里，最富的人表现极为出色。其他人总体过得还可以，但财富确实是向超级富豪集中——从920亿到2.3万亿，这个数字本身就说明问题。” 第四段：最低工资 vs. 收入所得税抵免断句： “But when it comes to wages, we’ve seen Walmart, for example, and some other companies follow in its footsteps, raising what they will pay their entry-level workers up to $10 by 2016.” “Last year when I asked you, Warren, if the federal minimum wage should be raised from $7.25 an hour, you said, ‘That is the toughest question you could ask me, because I’ve been thinking about it for 50 years and I don’t know the answer.’ And your reason for that is because you don’t know if more people will be better off, because you do lose some employment.” “I know if you increase it to $20, I’d like to see everybody make $20 an hour at a minimum, but I know if you increase it to $20 an hour, you’d have millions of people unemployed. I don’t know how to calibrate it precisely. I personally believe that the Earned Income Tax Credit is a much better way of handling the problem of people who are really not paid enough to live decently, and the Earned Income Tax Credit accounted for $56 or $57 billion in 2013. I would expand that a lot, and I would do it smarter too, but I think that’s more effective in helping the people who are really at the lower end than actually a change in the minimum wage.” 词汇分析： 表达 含义 follow in one’s footsteps 跟随某人的脚步/效仿 entry-level workers 入门级/基层员工 calibrate 精确校准、调整（这里指精确评估最低工资该定多高） live decently 体面地生活 the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) “劳动所得税抵免”，美国一项针对低收入劳动者的税收补贴政策 the lower end 收入底层人群 翻译： “但说到工资，我们看到沃尔玛这样的公司，还有一些跟风的企业，把入门级员工的时薪提高到2016年前达到10美元。” “去年我问你，联邦最低工资是否应该从7.25美元上调，你说：’这是你能问我的最难的问题，因为我已经想了50年，还是没有答案。’你说这是因为你不确定提高最低工资是否真能让更多人受益，因为这样做确实会导致一部分人失业。” “我知道如果把它提高到20美元——我确实希望每个人的时薪至少能到20美元——但我也知道如果真涨到20美元，会有几百万人失业。我不知道该怎么精确拿捏这个度。我个人认为，’劳动所得税抵免’（EITC）是解决’工作但收入不足以体面生活’这个问题的更好方式，这项政策在2013年的规模是560或570亿美元。我愿意大幅扩大它的规模，而且做得更聪明一些，但我认为，比起直接调整最低工资，这对真正处于底层的人帮助更大。” 第五段：为什么该关心收入不平等断句： “Why should people care about income inequality?” “Well, I think that we live in a country that has $54,000 of GDP per capita, and it’s the richest country in the world. And America, in many ways — real GDP is six times what it was per capita when I was born — but all kinds of people are left behind, and there are some structural reasons for that. And I think that a rich family takes care of the people that aren’t born with a particular wiring that enables them to prosper mightily in a market economy, and there’s lots of people that — they fight in Afghanistan, they do all — you know, through no fault of their own, their skills are not skills that the market values highly. And I think that a rich society, a very rich society, can figure out ways to have those people do better than they are.” 词汇分析： 表达 含义 GDP per capita 人均国内生产总值 be left behind 被落下、被时代抛下 structural reasons 结构性原因 (particular) wiring 比喻用法，”天生的头脑构造/禀赋”，指与生俱来适应市场经济的能力 prosper mightily 极为兴旺发达 through no fault of one’s own 并非某人自身的过错 market values highly 市场高度看重（某种技能） 翻译： “为什么人们应该关心收入不平等？” “我认为，我们生活在一个人均GDP高达5.4万美元的国家，是世界上最富有的国家。而且从很多方面看，美国现在的人均实际GDP是我出生时的六倍——但各种各样的人依然被落在了后面，这背后是有一些结构性原因的。我认为，一个富裕的家庭会照顾那些天生没有具备在市场经济中大展身手的’先天禀赋’的成员；同样地，社会上也有很多人——他们在阿富汗打仗，他们做了很多事——他们的技能并非市场所看重的技能，这不是他们自己的错。我认为，一个富裕的社会，一个非常富裕的社会，是可以想办法让这些人过得更好的。” 第六段：政治献金与民主断句： “With Citizens United and other decisions that enable the rich to contribute really unlimited amounts, that actually tilts the balance even more toward the ultra-rich. So the ballot box is the ultimate answer for changes in policy, but the unlimited giving to parties and to candidates really pushes us more toward a plutocracy. You know, they say it’s free speech, but somebody can speak 20 or 30 million times, and my cleaning lady can’t speak at all.” 词汇分析： 表达 含义 Citizens United 指2010年美国最高法院著名判例”公民联盟案”，裁定放开企业/团体的政治献金限制 tilt the balance 使天平倾斜，打破平衡 the ballot box 投票箱，代指”选举制度/民主投票” plutocracy 富豪统治、财阀政治 free speech 言论自由（此处巴菲特讽刺地用它来指代”花钱等于说话”） 翻译： “随着’公民联盟案’等一系列判决允许富人几乎无限制地捐款，这实际上让天平更加向超级富豪倾斜了。投票箱本应是政策改变的最终途径，但政党和候选人可以无限制地接受捐款，这实际上正把我们推向一种’财阀统治’。他们说这是言论自由，可问题是，有人能’说话’两三千万次，而我家的清洁工阿姨却一句话都说不了。” 第七段：股市与希腊退欧断句： “You said this year: periodically financial markets will become divorced from reality — you can count on that. Are US markets that way right now?” “Not yet, but they’ve moved a long way up, and they could get — I mean, we could have overpriced stock markets. We’ve had them at various times in the last 150-plus years, and we’ll have them again. It’s always easier to identify them in retrospect. When the market went on the S&P from 666 or so to 2100, I mean, that is a big move, but stocks were very cheap then. They might be a little on the high side now, but they’ve not gone into bubble territory.” “What about a tech bubble? Are we living 1999 all over again? The Nasdaq’s right near that 5,000 level.” “It’s a different composition to some extent now. Apple deserves a lot — they were eyeballs then, and they’re profits now in many cases. I do not regard us as being in bubble territory, but I don’t find cheap stocks to buy either.” “Do you think we will see a Greek exit from the Eurozone?” “I don’t know whether we’ll see it. I do know that the euro has had certain structural weaknesses since it was formed — that doesn’t mean it isn’t a good idea, it doesn’t mean that they can’t be corrected. But putting together a group of countries with significantly different fiscal policies, labor laws, cultures, and then trying to tie them all to a single currency can present strains as you go down the road, and as we’re seeing — they either have to learn to harmonize some other important economic characteristics of the countries more, or they can’t all stay on a common currency.” 词汇分析： 表达 含义 divorced from reality “脱离现实”，指市场价格脱离基本面 overpriced / underpriced 估值过高/过低 in retrospect 事后回顾来看 bubble territory “泡沫区域”，指资产价格已进入泡沫状态 eyeballs (互联网泡沫术语) 指1999年互联网公司靠”流量/点击量”而非实际盈利估值 Grexit（隐含） “希腊退出欧元区”的俗称（文中未直接出现该词，但语境即此） harmonize （政策、法律等）协调一致 fiscal policies 财政政策 翻译： “你今年说过：金融市场会周期性地脱离现实，这是必然的。美国市场现在是这种状态吗？” “还没有，但已经涨了很多，也可能——我是说，我们确实可能出现估值过高的股市。过去150多年里，我们经历过好几次这种情况，未来还会再出现。这种泡沫总是事后看更容易辨认。标普500从666点左右涨到2100点，这确实是很大的涨幅，但那时候股票非常便宜。现在可能有点偏高了，但还没有进入泡沫区域。” “那科技股呢？我们是不是又回到1999年了？纳斯达克现在接近5000点。” “现在的构成成分已经有所不同了。苹果这样的公司值这个价——1999年那批公司靠的是’流量’，现在很多公司靠的是实实在在的利润。我不认为我们处于泡沫之中，但我也确实找不到便宜的股票可买。” “你认为希腊会退出欧元区吗？” “我不知道会不会发生。我知道欧元自诞生起就存在一些结构性的弱点——这不代表欧元本身不是个好主意，也不代表这些问题无法纠正。但把一群财政政策、劳动法律、文化都相差巨大的国家捆在一起，用同一种货币，长期下来必然会产生压力，而我们现在正看到这一点——这些国家要么在其他重要的经济特征上进一步协调统一，要么就无法继续共用一种货币。” 第八段：慈善、贫困与美国梦断句： “What is the best thing that can be done to reduce poverty on a global scale?” “At the Gates Foundation, we think that health is probably the number one thing. I mean, if you aren’t healthy, and you don’t have access to vaccines and other aids to better health, you really don’t have anything going for you.” “You’ve pledged almost all of your wealth to philanthropy — 99% plus — and a lot of other billionaires have joined in that with you. What global issues can be solved through philanthropy, not just relying on the marketplace or capitalism?” “We won’t solve anything in the ultimate — I mean, we’re never going to get 7 billion people all as educated as we’d like, or all as healthy as we’d like — but things can be done in a major way in terms of health, in terms of family planning, in terms of education. And you try to figure out — if you really believe that every human life is of equal value, that means a different thing in some impoverished nation than it means in the United States, and you simply try to improve the lot of humans wherever they may be, just like your own children.” “Is the American Dream still alive and well?” “The American Dream is alive and well, but it isn’t for a good many people. It’s been alive and well for a lot of people, but there are people that — the American Dream is based in part on a market system and the rule of law and equality of opportunity, but a market system is going to leave a lot of people behind, and that’s where government comes in — that’s why we put in Social Security and some things of that sort. The American Dream, in the sense that anybody can move up into some top economic class, or become president of the United States — that is a dream, and social mobility has always been relatively good in this country compared to the rest of the world. But there are limitations to the American Dream: if someone is born with subnormal intelligence, they can have some dreams, but they’re not going to move into the top economic class, in all probability, unless they happen to be the child of some super-rich person.” 词汇分析： 表达 含义 have access to 能够获取/使用 have something going for you “有奔头/有依靠”，口语表达 pledge one’s wealth to philanthropy 承诺将财富捐给慈善事业 in the ultimate 从终极意义上说 the lot of humans “人类的命运/处境”（lot作名词表示”境遇”） alive and well （事物/理念）依然存在且有活力 rule of law 法治 equality of opportunity 机会平等 Social Security 美国”社会保障”制度（养老/福利体系） social mobility 社会流动性 subnormal intelligence 低于正常水平的智力 翻译： “从全球范围看，减少贫困最好的办法是什么？” “在盖茨基金会，我们认为健康可能是第一位的。如果一个人身体不健康，又无法获得疫苗和其他改善健康的手段，那他基本上就没什么指望了。” “你已经把几乎全部财富——99%以上——都承诺捐给了慈善事业，很多其他亿万富翁也跟你一起这样做了。有哪些全球性问题是可以靠慈善解决的，而不只是依赖市场或资本主义？” “从终极意义上说，我们解决不了任何问题——我是说，我们永远无法让70亿人都接受到我们理想中的教育，或都拥有理想中的健康水平——但在健康、计划生育、教育这些方面，我们是可以做出重大改变的。你要想明白一件事：如果你真心相信每一个人的生命价值都是平等的，那么这句话在一个贫困国家和在美国的含义是不一样的，你只是单纯地想改善各地人们的处境，就像对待自己的孩子一样。” “美国梦还存在吗，还有活力吗？” “美国梦依然存在、依然有活力，但对很多人来说并非如此。它对很多人来说一直有活力，但也有一些人——美国梦部分建立在市场体系、法治和机会平等之上，但市场体系必然会让很多人掉队，这时候就该政府出手了——这也是为什么我们建立了社会保障制度之类的东西。’任何人都能跻身顶层经济阶层，甚至当上美国总统’这种意义上的美国梦，确实是一个梦想，而美国的社会流动性，相比世界其他地方，一直算是相对不错的。但美国梦也是有局限的：如果一个人生来智力低于正常水平，他可以怀抱一些梦想，但他大概率无法跻身顶层经济阶层——除非他碰巧是某个超级富豪的孩子。” 整理自 English / Passage 16 One-on-One with Warren Buffett。本页于 2026-09-28 整理发布。

title: How AI Became More Expensive Than The Workers It Replaced
summary: 讨论人工智能使用成本上升，以及投入与实际产出的关系。
text: SummaryThis video questions the promise of cheap AI by examining rising usage costs. The notes discuss company adoption, token-based incentives, excessive consumption, and the difficulty of judging whether greater AI spending produces useful work. Watch on YouTube Content 以下为原笔记中的视频转录与学习内容，保留原素材的叙述语境。 In 2022, ChatGPT was released to the market, and since then the growth of AI has been impressive: the creation of hyperrealistic images, code generation, and even the delegation of complex tasks. AI seemed capable of doing everything with great ease, and after seeing everything it was capable of, companies began adopting AI exponentially. They incorporated it into their processes and realized that it was extremely cheap. But precisely because of its low costs, AI also began to bring problems. An AI company called Anthropic is raising alarms tonight about AI’s potential impact on employment that could soon be felt: thousands of layoffs, team reductions, and massive displacement. Literally, AI was eliminating jobs across every industry, from roles in tech companies — Amazon, Chegg, Microsoft, Meta, Salesforce, the list continues — tech companies just are cutting tens of thousands of jobs, to fast food chains. You could soon be ordering from an AI machine instead of a real person, the fast food company’s owner announcing today that artificial intelligence will work the drive-thru at hundreds of locations by the end of this year. AI was wiping out almost any type of job it could perform, the work of entire teams in just minutes, largely because it was much more efficient, but above all because it was cheaper to maintain. But in recent months a problem has started to emerge: AI is becoming very expensive. Because AI, maybe, is becoming too expensive to scale. Using OpenClaw these days is like driving a Ferrari — so much so that Microsoft itself banned its own employees from using Claude Code due to its high cost. So Microsoft starts cancelling Claude Code licenses. But this is not only happening at Microsoft — Uber, Nvidia, Amazon, and hundreds of other companies have reported similar cost problems, making it almost impossible even for top executives to justify such a high expense. Big tech is scrambling to slow down its use of AI. Major companies have already exhausted their annual budgets, and some say it’s getting more difficult to justify the costs. But if AI promised to be so cheap and efficient, how did it end up costing more than the workers it replaced? Although the birth of artificial intelligence dates back to the beginning of the 1950s, it was not until 2022 that this technology truly experienced a boom. It promised efficiency and solutions to complex problems with just one click, but most importantly, it promised to save companies a lot of money. From technology companies to fast food chains, every business began implementing it at an unprecedented speed. It was such a revolutionary technology that it could do the work of 10 people at one-tenth of the price — or at least, that was what people were saying. “AI is a technology for taking away your job, and maybe eventually displacing human sovereignty over our own future.” Starting in 2023, companies began not only encouraging but also forcing their employees to use AI tools, causing demand for these models to grow uncontrollably. And the way companies measured their AI performance and usage was through tokens. Using a high number of tokens became somewhat of a status symbol among employees, proving that they were going above and beyond to meet key performance indicators. But there was a problem: after realizing this, employees began using these tokens excessively simply to appear more efficient at the end of the month. This gave rise to what became known as “token maxing.” “Token maxing, like, that’s actually the coolest thing you can do now — token maxing.” And this new way of building, the token maxing, is expensive. For text-based inquiries the math is simple, with 750 words costing 1,000 tokens, and generating videos, images, code, and more can cost much more. By the end of 2025, token maxing began becoming popular among tech companies, making it increasingly common for software engineers to use AI even for insignificant tasks. But much of this popularity was driven by statements like these: “That $500,000 engineer, at the end of the year I’m going to ask him, how much did you spend in tokens? And that person said $5,000 — I will go ape. Something else, yes, right — if that $500,000 engineer did not consume at least $250,000 worth of tokens, I am going to be deeply alarmed.” Interestingly, Nvidia’s CEO, one of the companies benefiting the most from AI adoption, strongly encouraged all developers to use these tokens. The problem is that all this demand did not correspond to real demand, but rather was artificially inflated. Believe it or not, Silicon Valley engineers are now being scored on how many AI tokens they use — the problem that may end up inflating overall AI demand. At the same time, shortages of electronic components needed for building data centers are causing many of these projects to be delayed. According to Bloomberg, nearly 50% of all data center construction projects planned for 2026 in the US have been cancelled or delayed. But many of these constructions and plans were based on the enormous demand that AI companies were receiving. According to the Economic Times, demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure continues to greatly exceed supply. The thing is, experts are now beginning to question how much of this demand actually comes from real usage and how much comes from inflated figures. “So when a hyperscaler like Andy Jassy at Amazon, in his annual letter this morning — or that deal this morning — tells Wall Street that demand is outstripping supply, you got to ask: how much of that is real enterprise adoption, and how much is engineers juicing a leaderboard?” The problem is that due to token maxing, the cancellation of data center construction projects, and the massive adoption of AI worldwide, the cost of those tokens has increased significantly. “Onto concerns over the rising cost of artificial intelligence — it led to a major tech stock sell-off that dragged down the S&P and NASDAQ, which fell more than 500 points.” According to Bloomberg Finance, the average cost of tokens from large language models, or LLMs, has more than doubled since 2025. In December of that year the average cost was $1.11 per million tokens, and by May 2026 that number had reached $2.12 per million tokens. While this increase in price may seem insignificant, when taking into account the massive amount of tokens these companies use every day, it translates into tens of millions of dollars per month. “Employees in the company use about $200 worth of tokens every week, 50 weeks a year — that’s 10,000 bucks in tokens. You have 40,000 employees, that’s $400 million. You have 90,000 employees, that’s $900 million.” AT&T, for example, reported that it was consuming nearly 8 billion tokens every single day. Without a doubt, this has been incredibly profitable for Anthropic and OpenAI, the leading AI companies in the world today. According to Reuters, thanks to the adoption of AI agents at the enterprise level, Anthropic aims to nearly triple its annualized revenue in 2026. To put that number into perspective, in 2025 Anthropic ended the year with revenue of around $3 billion, and in 2026 that figure is expected to reach nearly $9.6 billion. But as a result, employers are frequently blowing through their AI budgets, putting them in a situation where it’s no longer clear that using AI is cheaper than hiring people — and AI companies are beginning to realize this. “The AI bill has come due. Annual budgets blown through in weeks, and now companies are facing a choice nobody has ever had to make before: tokens or humans.” An internal memo from a Microsoft executive vice president instructed engineers to stop using Anthropic’s AI coding tools. At first, executives said it was to encourage the use of AI tools within the same ecosystem, such as GitHub Copilot, but later it was discovered that the main reason was the enormous costs generated by the use of Claude Code. And Microsoft is not alone in this, as Fortune reports that other companies are also pulling back on AI usage. For example, Reuters reported that Meta consumed nearly 60 trillion tokens in a single month — that’s roughly $900 million worth of Anthropic’s tokens based on the firm’s blended prices. “If techno costs what humans cost, every company in America is about to start asking which one to keep.” But these extra costs are becoming a real headache for corporate finance departments. In fact, a Gartner survey found that three-quarters of the executives it polled expect technology budgets to increase this year, and nearly half estimate double-digit percentage increases. A sizable chunk of that spending will go toward AI, which is expected to account for more than one-fifth of total enterprise technology spending by 2035. And the numbers prove it: global spending on AI agents and models is rising at concerning rates. By 2027, spending on this technology is estimated to reach $680 billion — more than double what companies spent in 2025. But these estimates were made using the current average costs of these tools, and considering that both Anthropic and OpenAI are still not profitable — they are operating at a loss — that is about to change, because in the coming months both companies are expected to go public and will have to answer to shareholders. Therefore, they will inevitably increase the prices of using tokens from their AI tools and agents in order to generate profits. In other words, the amount of money companies are currently paying for tokens will multiply exponentially. So if the cost of using these tools continues to rise, there will come a point where hiring people becomes cheaper than paying the price of tokens. The thing is, this is not a prediction — in fact, this is already happening. “Maybe human labor will be more cost-efficient after all. Uber and Microsoft are starting to second-guess aggressive AI adoption. That’s partly because the cost of using AI can exceed the cost of human employees.” According to Reuters, the current cost of running AI agents is already comparable to the cost of human labor, and in some cases it is already more expensive. While in coding tasks the use of AI is undeniably cheaper, in data entry tasks the difference is minimal, but in others, such as call centers, the cost of human labor is actually cheaper. Although AI companies have so far been able to subsidize the real cost of tokens due to generous and abundant funding, that appears to be coming to an end. According to the Wall Street Journal, enterprise customers are beginning to question the true return on these investments. And the reality is that with the public listings of Anthropic and OpenAI, combined with investor pressure to see returns and electronic component shortages, this creates the perfect formula for token costs to continue increasing. And if maintaining these models is already expensive today, there will come a point when companies start asking themselves whether it makes sense to pay more for a simple tool than what they used to pay many of the workers they laid off. 整理自 English / Passage 15。本页于 2026-09-28 整理发布。

title: Something is seriously off and millions are noticing...
summary: 讲者关于昆虫、食品、气温、光污染和生活节奏变化的个人观察。
text: SummaryThe speaker reflects on gradual changes in everyday surroundings, including insects, food, summer heat, and the feeling that familiar patterns have shifted. These notes preserve the speaker’s observations and interpretation in a punctuated English transcript. Watch on YouTube Content 以下为原笔记中的视频转录与学习内容，保留原素材的叙述语境。 Have you ever had the feeling that something is different, but you can’t quite figure out what it is? Not one big thing, but lots of little things. Maybe you’ve noticed more ticks, hotter nights, food that just doesn’t taste the same. Maybe you’re not seeing as many bugs on the windshield when you’re driving down the road, or fields that used to be full of fireflies are empty. Most of these things haven’t changed overnight. They’ve happened slowly, over time, which has made it harder for us to notice them — until one day we look around and we notice that the world that we used to live in is almost non-existent anymore. The more people I talk to, the more I realize that I am not the only one that is feeling this. So many people seem to be looking around and noticing the same things. And I don’t think it’s nostalgia, and I don’t think that everything used to be perfect, but the life that used to feel normal to us is suddenly not feeling normal at all. So today I want to share some of the biggest observations that I have made, and you can let me know in the comments if you have noticed these too, or what other things you have noticed. The first one is just the amount of bugs. I remember when we used to go on vacation, we would drive from Tennessee down to the Gulf Shores, Alabama. It was like an 8 to 10 hour drive, and we would have to stop three to four times on our way down there to clean off our windshield, because it was covered — so just, like, full of bugs that you couldn’t even see out of the windshield. But as an adult, even driving around at night, you just don’t get the same amount of bugs on the windshield. And this is even in a rural area, where there should be tons of bugs. The same thing with fireflies. When I was a kid, we used to catch fireflies all the time, all summer long, and me and all the neighborhood kids would go in the evenings and catch — we would take empty peanut butter jars that were clear, and we would fill up the peanut butter jars with hundreds of fireflies. And I was four, I wasn’t great at catching the fireflies, I would guess, but it was very easy to fill up an entire jar. And today, you just don’t see that amount of fireflies anymore. At the same time, the tick population is exploding. I have seen videos of how bad ticks have gotten all across the US, and this is a huge issue, because the ticks that are around now are also carrying very high amounts of Lyme disease and other bacteria that is making people sick. When we were living in Virginia, we had some property — both me and my dog got Lyme disease at the same time and had to be treated, and all of that. We got Lyme disease and one other type of bacteria, I can’t remember what it was called, but the ticks, especially in like the northeastern part of the United States, are becoming very dangerous and abundant. And then we also have this new alpha gal syndrome, which is making people actually allergic to meat protein and is causing people not to be able to eat meat. There’s a lot of theories around why the tick population is exploding so much. Some of the theories are it’s caused by man intentionally — it’s, it’s a man-made problem. But then also, you just have hotter weather, longer warm seasons, it’s not dipping below freezing for as long as it used to, and so the ticks just have the natural ability to be able to spread. So we’re kind of living in a world right now where the dangerous insects — ticks and even mosquitoes — those populations are increasing, while the beneficial bugs and insects, their populations are decreasing. A lot of people talk about how food just doesn’t taste the same anymore. Tomatoes, strawberries, peaches — all of these foods kind of taste bland. It’s kind of like everything has just been muted, and we can’t quite taste the flavors that are supposed to be there. A lot of that has to do with our over-farming — the food is literally not as nutritious as it used to be. We’ve depleted our soil, and then the food companies are adding all of these chemicals and extra ingredients and manufactured things to our food. And so our food is, quite honestly, not the same that it used to be. I’ve heard a lot of people say how summer nights feel different. At night, the temperature used to cool down, and you would wake up in the morning and things were crisp. But today, it just kind of stays hot all night long, in a lot of places where it used to get cool. And so you never really get that relief from the heat, especially in the summer. And when things are warm, it just, it just kind of stays hot and muggy all the time, which is causing people to need to run their air conditioning more, and just not enjoy the evenings nearly as much. And even the sun during the day is feeling more intense. It’s like it is hotter, and you can’t stay out in it as long. I know when I was a kid, I could stay outside in the sun all day long, and even without sunscreen, I wouldn’t get burnt. And I mean, I’m pretty, pretty white, but I could be out all day and my skin was able to protect itself. You know, this was back in the 80s and 90s, and sunscreen wasn’t pushed as much as it is today, so it was pretty normal. But today, it’s a lot easier to get burnt by the sun. It seems like everybody has to be a little bit more careful, and a lot of that comes from awareness that if you do burn, you are at a higher risk for skin cancer, and skin cancer rates are increasing. But also, at the same time, that people are being more cautious and being more aware of putting on sunscreen or putting on extra clothing, and it almost feels like that’s a necessity these days — to wear rash guards and to stay out of the sun — because for some reason, our bodies just aren’t able to protect us in a way that it, it used to. Being able to see the northern lights in very unusual places, all the way down to Florida — sometimes these northern lights are being able to be seen by people. When we were living in Virginia, we were able to see northern lights several times, which was extremely odd. You know, I — that was never even a possibility of something that I thought we would be able to see. It’s just something that was never heard of when we were growing up — being able to see the northern lights in Florida. You know, that was something that you had to travel to Canada or Alaska, or the northern states of the US, in Maine or Michigan or something like that. Going out at night now, even in some pretty rural areas, you just can’t see the stars in the same way that you used to, and a lot of this has to do with light pollution. But, you know, there are so many stars in the sky. I have some pretty vivid memories — I used to lay out in my yard at night and just look up at the stars, and I would see shooting stars all the time, and we looked at constellations and all of that. And it just seems like it’s not that easy to do anymore — you have to go way out into a very rural area to be able to see more than, you know, a few stars at night. And when we would go to the beach in the summer, we could see the Milky Way very clearly. You just can’t do that anymore — you have to go out into a very, very rural area. I don’t even think people realize anymore — kids growing up today — realize quite how many stars there are up there, but, or even the Milky Way. A lot of people have never even seen the Milky Way. One of the hardest things for me is the lack of silence in the world. Everything is so noisy, it’s hard to escape and get to a truly quiet, serene place. I think that’s one reason why I like to go hiking so much, is because you can get into the woods and into the forest, and the trees kind of mute all of the outside noise, and, uh, you’re kind of in this cocoon of just forest, and it’s not silent, but it is at least nature, and all of the outside noise of the world is, is blocked. But any city, any suburban area, any place where there’s anybody else around you, it is just very hard to have true silence anymore. This really can lead to a lot of overwhelm and not being able to ever disconnect from society. And, and noise is something that you kind of get used to, and you don’t necessarily hear it, you don’t hear a lot of the background noise, um, but it is something that your body is having to process and filter out. There just used to be so many more spaces where people could go that were silent. There wasn’t so much development and traffic and noise of just everyday life. Construction — even now, I’m sitting here in a very rural area with the rice fields of Thailand, and birds singing all around me, but there’s also somebody weed eating the, um, rice fields, so I’ve got this noise of just a weed eater, which, you know, he’s working, whatever, but it’s still, even in this rural area, it’s not silent, because of the machines and the equipment that we have in our world, and just — it’s everything’s constantly going. One of the strangest things, when I talk to people, that everyone seems to be identifying with, is how fast time seems to be moving and how quickly things are happening today. And, you know, yes, our perspective changes as we get older, because we have more time to compare it to, so the percentage of our life that a year is makes it seem as if it is shorter, because it’s a smaller percent of our life each year. And so our perception of time — it does make sense that things would speed up a bit. But also, just the world that we’re living in is so fast-paced, and everything is happening — you don’t really have enough time to just stop and be, and live in the moment, and be bored, and think about things, and just do things at a slower pace. And because we’re always so fast and rushing and just trying to get things done, it, it seems as if the way that we’re living our lives is making time go by faster. And you can let me know what your opinion is on why time might seem like it’s going so fast, but that’s just been my conclusion of why everything goes so fast. You know, we only have one life to live, so I personally would like for life to slow down just a little bit, and that’s one of the things I’ve been working on — is trying to slow everything down, so that I have more life to enjoy and to experience. I don’t want it to rush by. I — I need it to slow down a little bit. With all of these little tiny changes, it really does make something seem not quite right. I know that life is always changing and evolving, but the world that we used to live in really isn’t there anymore. And it’s not one big thing — I mean, the big things have happened and changed — but I think it’s the little tiny things that we need to pay attention to.
