The things that are most important are these little tiny signs that, that something is changing, and they’re the things that we really need to focus on. Most people are so wrapped up in all of the big things that we’re missing all the small things that are changing — fewer fireflies, fewer stars, less quiet, more screens, more noise, more stress. And I’m not saying I need the world to go back to the way that it was, but I feel like all of these things that have changed are important. They were important then, and they’re important now. And I want to figure out why things have changed, because when something feels not quite right, when something feels wrong, maybe that’s the canary in the coal mine — the red flag that we need to pay attention to. 整理自 English / Passage 14。本页于 2026-09-28 整理发布。

title: The Biggest Wealth Killers in Your 20s and 30s (Avoid At All Costs)
summary: 识别二三十岁时妨碍财富积累的习惯与财务选择。
text: SummaryThis video argues that major life choices can have a lasting effect on personal finances. It discusses location, emergency savings, divorce, lifestyle spending, salary versus equity, delayed investing, sunk costs, expensive debt, and car purchases. Watch on YouTube Content 以下为原笔记中的视频转录与学习内容，保留原素材的叙述语境。 My dad got divorced three times. He made good money, he worked hard, and did most of the right things financially — but he still felt like he was starting over at age 50. That’s because the biggest wealth killers aren’t always about what you spend, but more about the life decisions that can drain your bank account without you even realizing it. Today we’re discussing wealth killers to avoid in your 20s and 30s, and I promise that there are at least a few ones you’ve never heard of before on any other personal finance channels. Wealth Killer #1: Staying in the Wrong CityThe first wealth killer that I wanted to talk about today is just staying in the wrong city, and this is one that nobody really talks about. But geography might be one of the most important financial decisions that you could make. If you grew up somewhere and there’s just not a lot of industries that align with what you want to do in your career, or perhaps the median salary in your city is dramatically lower than what you could be earning somewhere else, then by staying there you are costing yourself money. A city that’s good for your wealth usually has a few parameters. Number one, it has really good career prospects, and number two, it has quality people — you want to surround yourself with people that are as ambitious as you are, with similar goals to yourself. If you’re able to start in a city with a competitive salary, that’s going to be huge, because if you compound that over time, that’s going to amount to a lot of wealth in your lifetime. The first salary that you ever get will become the anchor to every salary negotiation that you have in the future. Pretend you live somewhere in the middle of America — say Kansas City. Now, if you’re from Kansas City, I’m not trying to throw shade at you; I’m just trying to illustrate that the median household income in Kansas City is $69,000 a year. If you were to move to Austin, Seattle, Boston, or San Francisco, the median jumps quite a bit. Austin has a median household income of $90,000 per year, and San Francisco is over $135K, just as examples. Even if your cost of living goes up somewhat, if you can keep it reasonable, you’re basically arbitraging the geographic difference in salary every year. A few years ago I visited a gold factory in Switzerland, out of all places, and what was really fascinating was that it was really close to the Italian border. A lot of people that worked in the factory were from Italy itself, just across the border. They wanted to work in Switzerland because the wages there were just that much higher. So what you had were Italian workers going into a Swiss gold factory, and then they could take that wage and go right across the border back to their hometown in Italy, where the cost of living was much cheaper. That’s an extreme example, but it’s the same principle of geographic arbitrage. The other thing that’s underrated here is your network. I really do feel like you can make a lot of money based on the quality of your network and the people that you meet. The opportunities we get exposed to and the introductions we receive — all of that is going to be highly dependent on where you actually live. You can always move back to your hometown once you’re established, but building your career in a low-opportunity city by default is a huge wealth killer that many people don’t even talk about or think about, and it happens a lot in your 20s and your 30s. Wealth Killer #2: Overfunding Your Emergency ReservesThe second wealth killer that we need to address is overfunding your emergency reserves, and a lot of you guys watching right now might fall into this trap because you want to be good with your money. In a typical emergency fund, you want to have between 3 to 6 months of living expenses saved up just for emergencies — that’s so that in case you lose your job, you still have some funds to rely on so that you can pay your bills, live your life, and find a new job. But I personally know people that keep $80,000, $100,000, $167,000 in a high-yield savings account just because, number one, it makes them feel better, and number two, they like the idea of having a really big buffer between them and a catastrophic emergency. But when you have 16 to 24 months of expenses parked in cash — or even more — that excess money is costing you money in terms of opportunity cost. Say your monthly expenses are $4,000 a month. A 6-month emergency fund would be $24,000, and a 16-month one would be $64,000. The difference there is $40K, and that extra $40K sitting in a high-yield savings account at 3.5% instead of being invested in the market at roughly 8 to 9% could cost you about $145,000 over 20 years. The point here is just to be intentional about how much you actually need. Anything beyond 6 months that you’re holding in cash “just in case” could just be a symptom of having a scarcity mindset. I definitely get it if you want to be safe with your money, but just make sure you’re not being too safe. Wealth Killer #3: DivorceAll right, this next wealth killer is probably the most uncomfortable one on this list to talk about, and that is divorce. Now, just to be upfront — I am not married, guys. I have no business lecturing anyone on relationships. But I did watch my dad get divorced three times, as I mentioned earlier. I personally had a front-row seat to two out of the three divorces: the first one was my mom’s, and the second was his third marriage. Every single time he got divorced, it set him back financially quite a bit. In fact, he would always tell me, “Son, I would be so much more wealthy if I didn’t get divorced.” And I think that really emphasizes the fact that finding a good partner is one of the most important decisions of your life. The US has the sixth highest divorce rate in the world, with 40 to 50% of married couples filing for divorce. The stat that’s even crazier is that second and third marriages have a divorce rate of 60% and 73% respectively — meaning that if you get divorced the first time, the likelihood that you get divorced a second or a third time is much, much higher. And you’d think with all these divorces that people would get prenups, but that’s actually not the case either, because only 15% of married couples report signing a prenup. Here are the top reasons for a divorce: lack of commitment at 75%, infidelity at 60%, too much conflict at 58%, and financial problems and getting married too young sit between 37 and 45%. So why is this such a wealth killer? Well, obviously the cost of the divorce itself is quite expensive — it can easily run you over $20,000. But the hidden costs of divorce are actually what add up to a lot more, in my opinion. Let’s say, for example, you own a home together. If you were to split up, that often means you have to refinance the house at whatever the current interest rate is — which, as we’ve seen recently, has not been good. The other option is that you just sell the house, and perhaps you’re forced to sell it during a bad market and you could lose a lot of money that way. Then, if you have retirement accounts, you have to split those, and those require a specific court order — you might even face taxes and penalties for early withdrawals. Don’t forget about moving costs as well, and if you want to split up furniture or physical assets, that can take a toll. And if either one of you owns a business that was started during the marriage, that can get very, very complicated too. If you add up all the hidden costs plus the normal cost of divorce via legal fees, it could run you up to $50,000 to $100,000 — and even sometimes more if you have a lot to lose. The bottom line is that who you marry is, unfortunately and fortunately, one of the most consequential financial decisions in your life. You want to get it right, but if you get it wrong, you could undo a lot of the wealth building that you made in your early years. Wealth Killer #4: Trying to Look RichThe next wealth killer you’ll probably encounter in your 20s and 30s is trying to look rich. There’s a phrase in the financial world that’s been around for decades, and it’s called “keeping up with the Joneses.” The reason why this phrase has stuck around is because it describes one of the most fundamentally destructive behaviors that we all fall for — and that behavior is trying to keep up with your friends. When you’re going through life, it’s natural to want to measure your own financial success against what other people appear to have, like your neighbors, your friends, or just people on Instagram. But if you do that, that’s when you’ve lost. A lot of what you see is what people want you to see — either in person or online — and that’s usually controlled and calculated, as long as they’re aware of their image. All you see is a highlight reel, but what’s really going on behind the scenes of someone’s life is something that you don’t really have access to. The new car might be leased, the designer clothes could be borrowed, and the apartment that looks super bougie and chic on Instagram might be taking up 60% of that person’s take-home pay. So there’s this term in Texas called the “30K millionaire” that I’ve talked about in another video, and that’s actually what we want to avoid being. The 30K millionaire is an individual who makes $30K a year but acts like they make millions — essentially doing everything in their power to flex on other people. According to Urban Dictionary: “Someone who goes to the club and pays to get the VIP table, but then they can’t buy any drinks because they spent all the money on the table.” What a 30K millionaire. The lesson here is that the people that look like they have money don’t have any money, and the people that don’t look rich are usually the ones that are mega rich. I personally think that if you’ve been building wealth for a long time by staying focused, staying in your lane, and living below your means, you’re going to get wealthier than someone who is trying to constantly compare themselves to others. Wealth Killer #5: Optimizing for Salary Instead of EquityThe next huge wealth killer in my opinion, in your 20s and 30s, is optimizing for salary instead of equity — especially if you have access to equity. This one is super relevant if you’re working for a startup or a company that offers stock-based compensation, but it’s also important enough to talk about in general as well. A lot of jobs these days — especially if you’re working for a public company, a startup, or perhaps a company on its way to IPO — are going to offer you equity as part of your total compensation. During the negotiation process, you usually have a little bit of flexibility. You can either opt for a high base salary and less equity, or you can have more equity and less of a base salary. A lot of people opt to take the higher base salary because they want that cash in hand, which gives them more cash flow and allows them to perhaps rent a nicer apartment or inflate their lifestyle a little bit. But here’s the thing: a single good equity outcome can actually outperform an entire decade of salary — or more. Of course, this is very dependent on where you work. I definitely understand that not everyone is going to work for a company like SpaceX, Google, or Nvidia. But in most cases, if you’re offered some sort of equity at a midsize to large company and you believe in that company, it’s my personal opinion that you should be taking more equity than cash — because at least there’s some upside with equity. Now, of course, this all comes with a huge disclaimer, which is that you have to do your due diligence on the company itself and whether it’s actually going anywhere. If your friend has a brand-new startup run out of his garage, you might want to think twice about the risk that comes with that. When it comes to figuring out what your potential equity is worth, I would do two things. First, figure out what your equity is worth as a percentage of the company. If a company offers you 10,000 shares, that’s not very meaningful unless you know how many shares are actually outstanding. If you do the math and figure out how much your shares are worth in terms of equity — you can get the total share count from your HR or legal department — then you can figure out what percentage of the company you own. Then you can do step two, which is to figure out what your company is worth currently, or what it will be worth in the future if it ever has a liquidation event or an IPO. If you own 0.1% of the company and your company ends up IPOing for $100 million, then your equity is worth 0.1% of that, or $100K. If you need more practice with that sort of thing, you might want to watch the Shark Tank show, because they actually often walk through valuation numbers quite often, and I think if you watch that show enough, you start to get it through repetition. Wealth Killer #6: Staying on the Sidelines When It Comes to InvestingThe next wealth killer is staying on the sidelines when it comes to investing. Now, if you are a returning viewer on this channel, you’ve probably heard me talk about this concept before. When we wait around to invest, that’s the most guaranteed way of not making any money. Here’s the hypothetical growth of $10,000 invested in the S&P 500 index from 1996 to 2025. You can see that if you’re fully invested all the days, your balance would be over $192,000. But if you miss just the 10 best days in that time period, your gains would be 56% less. The chart actually gets way worse: if you miss 20 of the best days, your gains are 74% less, and if you miss 30 of the best days, you’re looking at 84% less gains. Your portfolio growth is influenced heavily by being invested on the best performing days of the market, so you really can’t afford to lose any of those best days. Unless you are retiring soon and need to preserve your short-term wealth, it is often better to simply try to stay in the market as long as you can, rather than trying to time it for dips. I think so often many people just stay in cash, or they just want to wait till the market cools off a bit. I have a lot of friends that do this, but I think that if they aren’t at least earning the same rate as inflation, then their purchasing power is getting eroded by inflation itself. If you don’t want to invest for whatever reason, at the minimum you should keep cash in a high-yield savings account while the interest rates are decent. Wealth Killer #7: Sunken Cost LoyaltyNow, speaking of something that’s not decent, my next huge wealth killer is something called sunken cost loyalty. This wealth killer is about the tendency to stay at a job longer than you should, just because it’s comfortable, familiar, or you just like all the co-workers that you work with. But being loyal can actually be a double-edged sword — because if you stay at a company too long and they’re only giving you, let’s say, a 3 to 5% raise every single year, you’re just not going to make that much money, especially if you’re coming from a place where you started off with a low base salary. Let’s say you got a job out of college and you worked at, say, the Marriott Hotel Group, and you started off with a salary of $60,000 per year. At the core of it, every two years they will give you a cash raise of 3%. You work there for 10 years, and at the end of those 10 years your salary is $70,000 a year — and that’s not really a big pay bump, especially if you’ve been working for somewhere for 10 years. For me personally, I wasn’t the type of person to go into my boss’s office and demand a raise. I was personally taught that I was just lucky enough to have a job, especially because I graduated around the financial recession of 2008. And I’m sure many of you probably feel this way, especially because of all the layoffs that have been happening in America right now — you probably don’t want to rock the boat with your employer. But the reality is that companies are just not running around trying to give you raises left and right. They are going to give you exactly what they have to, and not a penny more. So if you don’t ask for a raise or stick up for yourself, you’re just volunteering to give up your potential value. One other strategy you could try to get out of this wealth killer is to switch jobs every couple of years, especially if you’re at the beginning of your career. If you’re able to switch jobs, you can reset the base salary when you do your negotiations, and usually this will result in a pay bump. According to a study from Lending Tree, workers who switched jobs saw their average earnings jump over 11%, and in some cases even upwards of over 30%. The idea here is that you want to be switching every 1 to 2 years, so that you either go laterally in job title and increase your pay, or you go laterally in terms of pay but increase your job title. Either way, as long as you’re consistently doing this and increasing your job title or your pay, by the time you are in your mid to late 30s your salary has been bumped up multiple times, and your wealth can continue its own growth. Wealth Killer #8: High-Interest Rate DebtThe next wealth killer on our list today — you know it quite well — is debt, especially high-interest-rate debt, and especially if you get into the wrong kinds of debt. Now, there are some cases in which borrowing money is actually okay, and I believe that not all debt is bad. I would argue that getting a mortgage to buy a home, or getting a student loan for a degree that pays off later — these are calculated uses of leverage. In these cases, you are borrowing money to acquire something that should appreciate or produce income for you in the future. So in those cases, I think that is pretty good debt. The problem in America is high-interest-rate debt, especially credit card debt or any debts that have an interest rate of over 10%. The average APR for credit cards is 22.11% as of 2026, and that means on a $10,000 credit card balance, you will pay roughly $185 in interest every month as part of your payment. If you have to pay these interest payments, then obviously you can’t use that money for anything else. Trying to build wealth for the future is going to be really tough, because a lot of your money is going to go straight to interest. So if you’re in your 20s or 30s, I think one of the best financial decisions that you can make is to never carry high-interest-rate debt from month to month — and this is just going to save you a lot of headaches in your life. Wealth Killer #9: Buying Too Much CarAll right, this next one you absolutely have to avoid, and it’s a famous one on my channel — and that’s buying too much of a car. If you’ve watched any of the other car videos on my channel, you will know that a car is a silent wealth killer, because not only are you paying car payments, but you have to pay hidden costs as well: insurance, maintenance, depreciation, and gas — those all add up over time. The average price of a new car in 2026 was over $51,000, which translates to a new car payment of over $750 a month, or about $9,000 a year. Then if you add in insurance and depreciation, the true cost of owning a car is easily over $1,000 a month. At an 8% average return, if you invested those payments instead, in 10 years it would be worth over $213,000. But that argument isn’t the best one, because it also assumes that you would give up driving a car altogether. So instead, may I suggest that you drive a reliable used car? The average used car payment is $537 a month — which is $213 less per month than the new car. You’re still going to have the same commute, and your life pretty much stays the same. But $213 a month invested over 10 years is worth over $45,000. That’s $45K for doing nothing different except choosing a used car over a new one. Our society attributes status and prestige to having a nice ride, and so much of our identity is wrapped into what kind of car that we drive. So if that’s the case and that’s you, and you still want to save some money, I still think it makes a lot of sense to buy a car that has around 30,000 miles on it, or is around 3 years used. You’re still getting a great deal on the car, you’re driving a car that’s not too old so it still seems brand new, and you’re going to save money on your total cost of ownership. So, out of all these wealth killers, which one do you identify with the most? Let me know in the comments. If you enjoyed this video, you’ll probably enjoy my video right here on the 10 things that are no longer worth your money in 2026 — it was one of my favorite videos to make this year, so make sure to check it out. I also have a new long-form YouTube show where I review my viewers’ finances. If you’re interested in seeing that show — where I talk to three different people per episode about their personal finances and try to fix them — you want to check that out as well. I personally think you would really enjoy that format, especially if you’re listening in the car or the gym. Thank you for being here. Peace. 整理自 English / Passage 13。本页于 2026-09-28 整理发布。

title: Lisa Su on Career Choices and High-Performance Computing
summary: 苏姿丰谈职业选择、技术发展与高性能计算。
text: SummaryIn this talk, Lisa Su reflects on her engineering education, career, and work at AMD. The notes connect long-term strategy, partnerships, chiplets, and AI with advice for students choosing their own path. The transcript is followed by business and technology vocabulary and a Chinese translation. Watch on YouTube Content 以下为原笔记中的视频转录与学习内容，保留原素材的叙述语境。 Um, first of all, President Chen, thank you so much for inviting me. Actually, you invited me several times to come to NTEU, and I was honored every time to come here. But sometimes when I come to Taiwan, it’s very, very busy, and especially around Computex timing, it’s always very busy. So this is actually a great time that I can visit, and you know, thank you for the warm invitation, and Professor Woo as well. Thank you so much. It’s really my pleasure to be here to meet all of you very talented students, and you make me feel very old, but hopefully I can give you a few stories for your career. So maybe I should say my background was in electrical engineering and computer science. That’s where I went to school — MIT — for bachelor’s, master’s, and PhD, and my specialty was semiconductor devices. So when I was a young student, that is what I studied. Now, for AMD, I’ve been in the semiconductor industry for over 30 years, and what you find is that the technology moves so fast. For AMD, I’ve been with the company since 2012, and CEO since 2014. And probably the most important thing with any company is to decide: what do you want to be when you grow up? And for AMD, my belief is that our specialty is in high performance computing. And high performance computing is really at the center of all of our lives today. I’d like to say that AMD’s technology touches billions of people every day — whether you’re talking about cloud data centers, or anywhere in the edge of the network, or PCs, or automotive, or industrial — you probably can touch some of AMD’s technology. But from a technology company standpoint, the most important thing is you have to have a long-term strategy and roadmap. And so our focus was really on three things. First is high performance computing. The second is to have really excellent partnerships — TSMC is at the center of our partnership overall. And then the third piece is that the semiconductor industry is changing, and many of you have heard that Moore’s law is slowing down and changing. And we made a big bet on chiplet technology as a very key area going forward. So these are some of the things that were important for AMD, and today I’m very happy to say that when you look at the top supercomputers in the world, five out of the top ten are based on AMD’s technology. And from that standpoint, I really feel that high performance computing is at the center of what’s most important going forward. So I heard that many students still view chip design as the most exciting thing. I would say that there’s always a movement — sometimes hardware is more exciting, sometimes software is more exciting. I think from my standpoint, the most exciting part of design is actually holistic design. You have to really design hardware, software, and systems together. Especially when we’re talking about AI going forward, you cannot design each piece separately. You actually have to think about what is the overall system application — especially thinking about the algorithms and the applications — and then you can think about how you want to design your chips. The one thing I can say about the AI industry is: every week there is new technology and innovation coming out. And I think DeepSeek was one of those moments when it came out in January. I think there was some surprise. And when you look at what they’ve done, it’s actually pretty clever technology — really gathering all of the different innovations, using the mixture-of-experts models, and so on and so forth. But the main thing that we saw with DeepSeek is: when you can find a way to make AI more accessible and actually cheaper, you actually will have more usage and application of AI. So the main thing that DeepSeek has done is it has really accelerated the application of AI. Of course, that’s not a market statement — that’s a technology statement. From everything that we see, the key point about AI is that there’s no one-size-fits-all for the computing ecosystem. You have the very large frontier models, where the few people who can invest at that level — hundreds of billions of dollars — are going to go as fast as possible because they want to build the best model. But you also find that that is just one application of AI. You also see there will be many different medium-sized models, smaller models, and people will use different algorithms to get there. So my expectation is that there will continue to be very significant investment — including very large investments as well as more affordable investments — going forward. So the most important thing I can say about AI is that the market is huge. We expect that the market over the next three or four years will be around 500 billion dollars. And in that type of market, you need all different kinds of computing. There’s no one company that has all of the solutions. My view is that you need every kind of computing — you need CPUs, you need GPUs, you need ASICs, you need FPGAs. And in that framework, I think our AI strategy is, number one, to have a very complete solution — a complete solution that includes hardware, software, and systems. And the second piece is to have an open ecosystem. One of the most important things is to foster collaboration and to have an open ecosystem, so that people can learn from each other. That was also another important part about DeepSeek — it was an open model, and as a result, many people innovated on top of that. So my answer is: the market is huge, and our AI business spans every aspect — from the largest data centers to even the PC level. We believe there will be a lot of AI, so there’s a lot of market for all of us. I think the Taiwan ecosystem is very special. When you look at it — starting from the TSMC ecosystem, which has really built this incredible manufacturing capability, and then including all of the ODM, OEM, manufacturing ecosystem, design ecosystem — I think more investment on the software and system side will come. From an AMD standpoint, we’re very proud of our team here in Taiwan, which is a very important piece of our overall R&D. But the other thing I would say is: in this world today, ecosystems are very interconnected. From a United States standpoint, I think we do rely on a lot of the Taiwan manufacturing ecosystem, and trying to build resilience into that ecosystem is important. I’m happy to say that I was born in Tainan, and my parents immigrated to the United States. And as you can imagine, that was a very big move for them. When we went to the US as a family, the key part that my parents always instilled upon me is: education is so important. So for all of you in school — I remember when I was at MIT, I very much wanted to finish school. After my bachelor’s degree, I actually thought I should finish school and go to work. And my parents said, “No, Lisa, you cannot do that.” They strongly, strongly suggested I get a PhD. At the time, I was very impatient. I was like, “Oh, school is enough. Maybe some of you feel the same way.” And the truth is, my parents were right — because what you get from your university and your graduate school is really an opportunity to learn many different things and to build the confidence to solve the future problems. So even though I was not happy with my parents at the time, I think they were absolutely right. And as for the experience of being CEO of AMD — I would say it was kind of my dream job, to start from a semiconductor engineer, to become a business person, and then become a semiconductor leader. But it was not easy, especially in those early years. My parents and family have always been very supportive of that, and I’m very lucky in that way. My thinking is that there are many different kinds of leaders, and we have a lot of respect for all kinds of leaders. But I truly believe that university education is so helpful. These years that you’re in university are really the best time to learn and to decide what you enjoy the most, so that you can decide your next step in your career. First of all, I have tremendous respect for Jensen — tremendous respect. I think as the founder of Nvidia, he has really built an amazing company. I would say that we run independent companies, though. Probably in the semiconductor industry, we do have a semiconductor industry association in the US where all semiconductor companies are present, and in that forum we would exchange some ideas. I can say that in my experience, one piece of probably the best advice I received from a mentor was: “Lisa, whatever you do, I would suggest that you pick the hardest problems.” The advice they gave me is to run towards problems. And I think that’s the best advice I can give students — because there are so many interesting things to do in the world, and choosing a project, a problem, or a company where you can make a big impact means you will learn so much and be able to contribute so much. And I can say for sure that I learned the most from the biggest mistakes I made. So mistakes are not a bad thing — mistakes are actually a good thing, because you can learn from those lessons and be better in the future. The political science question is not the easiest question — technology is actually a little easier. I think I would maybe not talk about individual countries, but talk a little bit about my thinking on AI. Because AI is such a new technology — if you think about the last few years, we’re all learning together. Countries are learning, companies are learning, individuals are learning. The initial thought process is that AI could be quite dangerous if there are not good guardrails. However, on the other side, you don’t want to stop innovation. From my standpoint, I think AI is the type of technology where we have to innovate and go as fast as possible, while understanding that there does have to be regulation — but not too much regulation, so that you slow down the progress. In general, that’s my philosophy. And I think countries that embrace technology are going to really benefit from it. Many countries around the world are all building their AI policies. I think everybody should be educated in AI. It doesn’t matter which department you’re in. When you say you’re in the literature and linguistics department, I think AI can also be very beneficial — to understand how to apply AI in your field. And most of what we see today is that people are still learning what they can use AI for in each field. So we talk a lot about the development of AI, but there’s also a whole field on the application of AI going forward. I would certainly encourage all students to explore that. I would say that Taiwanese-Americans and Taiwanese in general are extremely hardworking and really think about how to contribute to their fields and their professions. And I think that’s something we can be very proud of. Although some people say that I’m more American than Taiwanese, I’d like to think I’m Taiwanese-American. Probably the most difficult time for AMD was when I started in 2014. At that time, the company had a roadmap that was not competitive. If you’re in a technology company, your product is the most important thing — I would say that’s the number one thing. And so our goal was to really reframe our product roadmap. I had three priorities: the first was to build great products; the second was to have very, very deep customer relationships, because together in this world there’s no one company that has all the good ideas, and collaboration is very important; and the third is to be very agile and move very quickly. In that standpoint, our biggest job was to give ourselves time to build this great roadmap. And I am now happy to say our CPU roadmap is based on our Zen technology — we’re now on the fifth generation of Zen technology. We went from, let’s call it, not the best — to today, where I feel we have the best CPU technology in the world. And we also have a much broader roadmap going forward. So the key in those times is to be very clear about what you’re trying to achieve. For us, in a technology company, it is always to build great products — that’s the number one foundation. In terms of semiconductor trends, I would say we start with the idea that we have to have a very holistic design environment — hardware, software, and systems all need to be optimized together. Probably one of the most exciting parts about AI is that we’re still in the very early innings. I would say we still have probably ten years of very significant innovation in AI. And on the application space, we’re going to go from today — where we talk about AI making our businesses or people more productive — to, over the next many years, much larger changes in terms of what AI can do for us. Probably one of my most exciting or most interesting areas is healthcare and life sciences. I know that there’s a medical school here, and the application of AI together with medicine I think can help us solve things like curing diseases, finding new drug therapeutics, and diagnosing future health problems much sooner. That’s just one example of what AI can do going forward. I would encourage you to be very ambitious in what you would like to achieve. The most important thing for young students or those early in their career is: you can do anything. So have very big dreams. And if you tell people — tell your colleagues, your managers, your future mentors — people will help you achieve those opportunities. I would say that sometimes Taiwanese or Asian people are a little shy. So speak up. Share your dreams. When you have the right people, it makes all the difference — because not everyone has the same motivation. Some people are motivated by their project, some by starting a company, some by other reasons. At AMD, we try to have the right people to build that team. And for our engineers, when we started, we wanted to build the best — that was our ambition. But we also thought we should be very realistic: you cannot go overnight from not competitive to the best. You have to build a plan to do that. Engineers basically love to solve problems. We have to give them good problems to solve. We’re all motivated by seeing success — success comes in recognition of the product, great people wanting to join the company, and yes, revenue growth, which leads to market share growth, which leads to stock price growth. My personal opinion is that a PhD is actually pretty useful. During your PhD thesis, you work on a problem that nobody else is really working on in the world, and that gives you a lot of opportunity to explore much more broadly than sometimes you can in a company, where you become much more focused. So I actually think a PhD is pretty useful — but it’s different for every person. On the topic of soft skills: I would say the world changes very fast, so it’s important to be quite agile in your thinking. Maybe today you think this is the right path, but you will learn something every day. I have a big philosophy that says you need to continuously learn all the time. Every day you’re going to learn something new, and you can decide how you might change your path. That’s something I use very much, and it’s an important soft skill. And then on how you deal with setbacks — I said earlier you actually learn the most when you have a setback, a failure. I can tell you so many examples of my own setbacks. But my advice is: you can be sad for just a short time. Of course, we’re all human beings — if something didn’t go the way you wanted, you might be a little unhappy. But only for a very short time. And then after that, you learn, and you get really focused on your next thing. I think that’s the key. I can say for sure I’m just an okay student — okay meaning pretty good, but not A++. Maybe A-minus, that kind of thing. I actually think everyone is different, and the most important thing is to take whatever you learn and apply it in the real world. Even in device physics — a very, very hard class — I found that the written problems were very hard, but working in the lab on a project, I was really good. So everyone has their specialty. Let me say one thing: I’m a big believer that it’s not the number of people you have for anything — for a company, for a project — it’s whether you have the right people. When I first started at AMD, we had 8,000 people. People used to say, “Oh my goodness, you’re so small compared to Intel.” At that time, I think Intel had maybe ten times the people of AMD. And they said, “Lisa, you’re crazy. Why are you doing that? You cannot possibly win.” And I said, “Really? Why do you say that? I don’t feel that way. I don’t feel that it’s the number of people — I feel that it’s the right people, with the right project, with the right focus, and the right vision.” And to the point about how do you optimize — I think everyone has in their mind what they can see as their path, and every company’s path is different. From my standpoint, and maybe since this is the last question, I will make it a little bit broader: we are incredibly lucky to be in this technology field. I hope all of you feel this way. What I really enjoy about what we’re doing in technology is that the technology we’re working on is touching billions of people every day. It is having an impact on people’s lives. It will make companies better. It will make your life better. It will make our future healthcare better. It will make our future sustainability better. From all of those aspects, we’re very lucky to work on this type of technology. And so we have to find what is it that we’re going to do best. For us at AMD, it’s around high performance computing. I don’t believe that we can do everything — but I do believe that in high performance computing, it can have a very wonderful impact on people’s lives. And that’s what we choose to do. Vocabulary & Expressions以下精选演讲中有代表性的词汇和表达，按类别整理。 一、商业与科技术语 英文 中文释义 说明 high performance computing 高性能计算 AMD核心战略方向，简称HPC roadmap 技术路线图 科技公司常用词，指产品规划蓝图 holistic design 整体性设计 指硬件、软件、系统协同设计的思路 chiplet technology 小芯片技术 将芯片拆分为多个功能模块后再封装，AMD重要技术路线 Moore’s law 摩尔定律 每18-24个月晶体管数量翻倍的规律 mixture-of-experts (MoE) 专家混合模型 一种AI模型架构，DeepSeek使用的关键技术 frontier models 前沿大模型 指GPT-4、Claude等顶尖规模的AI模型 ASICs 专用集成电路 Application-Specific Integrated Circuits，专为特定任务设计的芯片 FPGAs 现场可编程门阵列 Field-Programmable Gate Arrays，可重新编程的芯片 ODM / OEM 代工设计商 / 原始设备制造商 台湾制造生态的重要组成 open ecosystem 开放生态系统 强调开放协作而非封闭垄断 guardrails 护栏、安全边界 比喻对AI技术的规范与约束机制 二、地道表达与习语1. “what do you want to be when you grow up” 字面意思是”你长大后想成为什么”，这里活用于企业层面 意思是：一家公司必须想清楚自己的核心定位是什么 中文可译为：”弄清楚自己想成为什么样的公司” 2. “we’re still in the very early innings” “inning”是棒球术语，指”局” 这里是比喻：我们还处于AI发展的早期阶段 类似中文说法：”才刚刚起跑”、”尚处于开局阶段” 3. “run towards problems” 直译是”朝着问题跑去” 实际含义：主动迎难而上，而不是回避困难 是Lisa Su从导师那里得到的最重要建议之一 4. “no one-size-fits-all” 字面意思：”没有一套适合所有人的方案” 商业语境中常用，意指：不存在放之四海而皆准的解决方案 5. “instilled upon me” “instill”意为”将……灌输/植入” “my parents always instilled upon me” = 父母一直向我灌输（某种理念） 6. “agile” 原意”敏捷”，在科技商业语境中特指：能快速响应变化、灵活调整方向的能力，也是一种软件开发方法论（敏捷开发） 7. “touching billions of people every day” 不是字面的”触摸”，而是比喻：影响着每天数十亿人的生活 这是Lisa Su反复强调AMD使命感的核心表达 8. “A-minus kind of student” 美国成绩评分体系：A+、A、A-、B+…… 意思是：成绩不错，但并非顶尖，强调并非天才、靠努力和实践见长 9. “that’s a market statement vs. a technology statement” Lisa Su区分两种性质的判断：技术层面的判断（客观分析技术影响）vs. 市场层面的判断（商业竞争预测） 这是她在谈DeepSeek时刻意区分的表达，显示商业谨慎 10. “resilience” 在供应链语境中指：韧性、抗风险能力 “build resilience into the ecosystem” = 增强生态系统的抗风险韧性 三、演讲风格词汇（口语化表达） 表达 功能 说明 “Let me say one thing” 引入重要观点 口语化的强调句式 “you know” 填充语 演讲中频繁出现，相当于中文”你知道吗” “from my standpoint” 表达个人立场 等同于”in my opinion”，但更正式 “to that end” 承接逻辑 “为此”、”为了这个目标” “back to the question” 回归正题 演讲中用来归位焦点 “I would say” 语气缓冲 表达观点时的谦和措辞 中文翻译首先，感谢陈校长的邀请——您其实已经邀请我来台湾大学好几次了，每一次我都深感荣幸。但我每次来台湾行程都非常紧凑，尤其是Computex前后，总是忙得不可开交。所以这次能专程过来拜访，真的非常难得。也要感谢吴教授，谢谢大家的热情款待。能在这里见到这么多优秀的学生，我由衷感到高兴——虽然你们让我觉得自己老了不少，但希望我分享的一些故事，能对大家的职业发展有所助益。 先介绍一下我自己的背景。我学的是电机工程与计算机科学，在MIT读完了学士、硕士和博士，专攻半导体器件。那时候年轻，读的就是这个。到了AMD，我已经在半导体行业深耕超过三十年了，这一路走下来最深的感受就是：技术迭代之快，超乎想象。我是2012年加入AMD的，2014年起担任CEO。 对任何一家公司来说，最重要的事可能就是想清楚一个问题：你到底想成为一家什么样的公司？AMD的答案在我看来很明确，那就是高性能计算。而高性能计算，正是当今所有人生活的核心。我常说，AMD的技术每天触达全球数十亿人——无论是云端数据中心、网络边缘节点，还是个人电脑、汽车、工业设备，你几乎都能找到AMD技术的身影。 但对于一家科技公司而言，最重要的事是要有长远的战略和技术路线图。我们的重点聚焦在三件事上：第一，高性能计算；第二，建立卓越的合作伙伴关系，其中台积电是我们最核心的战略伙伴；第三，正视半导体行业的变局——摩尔定律正在放缓，我们因此在小芯片技术上押下了重注，将其视为未来最关键的技术方向。 这些是AMD走到今天的基石。我很欣慰地看到，在全球最顶尖的十台超级计算机中，有五台采用的是AMD的技术。从这一点上，我深信高性能计算正是未来最重要的方向。 我听说很多同学仍然认为芯片设计是最令人兴奋的领域。我觉得这其实一直是在变化的——有时候硬件更热门，有时候软件更受追捧。但在我看来，最令人激动的其实是整体性设计——你必须将硬件、软件和系统作为一个整体来设计。尤其是在AI时代，各个部分根本不能割裂开来看。你必须从系统全局出发——先想清楚算法和应用场景是什么，再去思考芯片应该怎么设计。 关于AI行业，我可以说：几乎每周都会出现新的技术突破。DeepSeek在一月份发布的时候，确实让很多人吃了一惊。仔细研究它做的事情，其实技术上相当聪明——把各种创新整合在一起，混合专家模型等等。但DeepSeek带给我们最重要的启示是：当你能让AI变得更易获取、成本更低，使用量和应用场景就会爆发式增长。所以DeepSeek真正做到的，是大大加速了AI的落地应用。 当然，这是技术层面的判断，不是市场预测。从我们观察到的情况来看，AI计算领域并不存在一套放之四海而皆准的方案。顶尖的前沿大模型赛道上，少数能投入数千亿美元的玩家会全力冲刺，追求极致性能。但这只是AI应用的一种形态。未来还会涌现出各种中型模型、小型模型，人们也会用不同的算法路径来达到目标。因此我预判，未来既会持续有大规模的重磅投资，也会有越来越多平价高效的选择并存。 总体而言，关于AI最重要的一句话就是：市场足够大。我们预计未来三到四年，这个市场规模将达到五千亿美元。在这么大的市场里，需要各种各样的算力，没有哪家公司能包打天下。在我看来，CPU、GPU、ASIC、FPGA——各种计算方式都有其用武之地。在这个框架下，AMD的AI战略有两个核心：一是提供完整的解决方案，涵盖硬件、软件和系统；二是构建开放的生态系统，鼓励协作与共享，让大家能够互相借鉴。DeepSeek的成功也印证了这一点——正是因为它选择了开放，才引发了大量的二次创新。 所以说，市场很大，机会很多，AMD的AI布局从最大规模的数据中心延伸到个人电脑，各个层面都有所覆盖。这个领域足够大，足以容纳所有人。 我认为台湾的产业生态非常独特。从台积电构建起来的制造能力出发，再叠加上ODM、OEM、整个制造与设计生态，已经形成了强大的基础。未来我相信软件和系统层面的投资还会进一步加码。AMD在台湾的团队是我们全球研发体系中非常重要的一环，我们对此深感自豪。另外我也想说，今天的世界，各个生态系统之间高度相互依存。美国的确在很大程度上依赖台湾的制造生态，如何为这套生态系统建立更强的韧性，是一个重要的课题。 顺便说一句，我出生在台南，父母后来移民到了美国——那对他们来说是非常重大的一步。到了美国之后，父母一直给我灌输的核心理念就是：教育，至关重要。所以我想对在座所有还在学校里的同学说：我在MIT读书的时候，其实非常想赶紧毕业。拿到学士学位之后，我一度觉得应该去工作了。我父母斩钉截铁地说：”不行，Lisa，你必须读博。”当时的我非常不耐烦——“书够了，够了！”也许你们有人现在也有同样的感受。但事实证明，父母是对的。大学和研究生阶段给你的，是一段可以广泛学习、建立自信、锻炼独立解决问题能力的宝贵时光。当年我对父母的决定很不满意，但如今回头看，他们完全正确。 担任AMD CEO这段经历，可以说是我的梦想成真——从半导体工程师起步，成长为商界人士，再成为半导体行业的领军者。这条路走得并不容易，尤其是早期那些年。但父母和家人始终是我最坚实的后盾，我在这方面非常幸运。 我的看法是，优秀的领导者有很多种，每一种都值得尊重。但我真心认为，大学阶段的系统教育无可替代。你们现在在大学里的这几年，是最好的探索时光——弄清楚自己真正热爱什么，才能为下一步的职业选择打好基础。 说到黄仁勋，我对他有非常真诚的敬意——作为英伟达的创始人，他把这家公司做到了令人叹为观止的高度。当然，我们是各自独立运营的公司。在美国半导体行业协会的框架下，各家企业有时会在同一个场合交流一些看法。 说到我所收到过的最重要的职业建议——有位导师曾对我说：Lisa，不管做什么，要主动选择最难的问题。这句话的核心就是：迎难而上，而不是绕道而行。这也是我想送给在座同学的最重要的建议。这个世界上有太多有趣的事情可以做，但选择一个真正能让你产生重大影响的项目、问题或公司，你能从中学到的东西，以及你能作出的贡献，都将是无可比拟的。我可以坦诚地说，我从最大的错误中学到的东西最多。所以犯错并不可怕，犯错是一件好事——因为那些教训会让你越来越好。 关于各国AI政策的问题，这比技术问题复杂多了，我就不展开谈具体国家了。但我可以分享一下我对AI的整体看法：AI是一项全新的技术，过去这几年，所有人——国家、企业、个人——都还在摸索学习之中。一方面，如果缺乏必要的安全边界，AI确实可能存在较大风险；另一方面，我们又不希望因为过度管控而扼杀创新。我的立场是：AI是一种必须全力推进、加速创新的技术，同时也需要适度监管，但不能矫枉过正，阻碍进步。我相信，那些积极拥抱技术的国家，将会从中受益最深。各国正在纷纷制定自己的AI政策，这是一个非常动态的时代。 我认为，AI教育应该是面向所有人的，无论你在哪个专业。你说你在文学与语言学系，AI对你同样大有裨益——关键是学会如何将AI应用到自己的领域中。现阶段，大家普遍还在摸索各自领域里AI的用武之地。我们讨论了很多AI技术的开发，但AI的应用研究同样是一个广阔的方向。我非常鼓励所有同学都去探索。 台湾人，包括台湾裔美国人，给我的印象是非常勤奋，而且真心致力于在自己的领域里作出贡献——这是我们应当引以为豪的特质。虽然有人说我更像美国人，但我更愿意称自己是台湾裔美国人。 AMD最艰难的时期，大概是我2014年接手时的那段日子。那时候，公司的产品路线图已经完全失去竞争力。对于科技公司来说，产品是一切的根本，是重中之重。所以我们的首要任务，就是彻底重塑产品路线图。我当时给自己定了三个优先级：第一，做出卓越的产品；第二，建立深厚的客户关系——因为这个世界上没有哪家公司能独揽所有好点子，协作永远是必要的；第三，保持高度的敏捷性，快速行动。 在那段时期，最重要的事是争取足够的时间来完成这张路线图。今天，AMD的CPU架构建立在Zen技术的基础上，我们已经迭代到了第五代Zen。从当年的”竞争力不足”，到今天我可以自信地说，我们拥有全球最强的CPU技术。前提是你要对目标有清晰的认知——在科技公司里，建好产品永远是第一基础。 谈到半导体的技术趋势，我觉得起点还是整体性的设计理念——硬件、软件、系统必须协同优化。关于AI，我认为最令人兴奋的，是我们还处于非常早期的阶段，前面还有大约十年的密集创新期。在应用层面，我们会从今天的”帮助企业和个人提升生产力”，逐步走向更深远的变革。其中我个人最感兴趣、也最看好的领域是医疗健康与生命科学。我知道这里有医学院，AI与医学的结合，有望帮助人类攻克顽疾、发现新药、更早诊断潜在的健康问题——这只是AI未来能做到的事情的一个缩影。 我想鼓励大家：对自己的目标要有野心，要敢于做大梦。对于年轻学生或者初入职场的人来说，最重要的认知是——你可以做到任何事。所以大胆说出你的梦想，告诉你的同学、导师、未来的上司，大家都会愿意帮助你去实现它。我想特别说：华人或亚裔的学生，有时候会稍显内敛。要大声说出来，不要藏着掖着。 说到团队建设，我始终认为：关键不在于人多，而在于找对人。每个人的动力来源不同——有人热爱项目本身，有人想创业，有人有其他的驱动力。AMD的做法是找到合适的人，组建合适的团队。对于我们的工程师，我们从一开始就立志做到最好，但同时也保持清醒：从”不具竞争力”到”业界最强”，不可能一蹴而就，必须有一套扎实的计划。工程师的本质是热爱解题，所以你要给他们真正值得解的好题目。每个人都受到成功的激励——来自产品的认可、人才的加盟，也来自收入增长、市场份额扩大、股价提升。 关于读博士，我个人的看法是：非常值得。博士阶段你会深耕一个几乎没有人在做的问题，这种广度的探索，是进入企业之后很难得到的。所以我认为读博士很有价值——当然，每个人的情况不同。 软实力方面，我想说的是：世界变化太快，思维上的敏捷度非常关键。也许今天你认定了一条路，但明天你可能就会学到全新的东西。我有一个根深蒂固的信念：必须持续学习，每一天。每天都有新的东西值得学习，然后你再决定要不要调整方向。这是我非常重视的一种能力，也是我觉得最重要的软实力之一。 关于如何面对挫折——我之前说过，你往往从最大的失败中学到最多。我自己的挫折经历实在不少，但我的建议是：难过可以，但只能难过一小会儿。我们都是人，事情没有按预期发展的时候，心里会不好受，这很正常。但只能难过一小会儿，之后就要迅速从中汲取教训，把精力全部投入下一件事。这是最关键的。 我得坦白说，我只是一个还不错的学生——不是什么A++的尖子生，大概就是A-减的水平吧。我真心认为每个人都不一样，最重要的是把你学到的东西运用到现实世界中去。就拿器件物理来说，那门课对我来说非常难，书面考试让我很头疼，但一到实验室做项目，我就来劲了——每个人都有自己擅长的地方。 我一直有一个坚定的信念：做任何事，关键不在于人的数量，而在于有没有合适的人。AMD刚开始的时候只有8000名员工，很多人对我说：”天哪，你们跟英特尔比起来太小了，他们的人数可能是你们的十倍。你这是在瞎搞，根本赢不了。”我的回答是：”是吗？为什么？我并不这么认为。人数多少不是关键，关键是有没有对的人、对的项目、对的专注点、对的愿景。” 最后，关于如何优化与前进——每个人心中都有自己看得到的路，每家公司的路也都不一样。站在这个时间节点上，我想说得更宏观一点：我们能身处这个科技行业，真的是无比幸运。我衷心希望大家也有这种感受。我最热爱这份工作的原因是：我们所做的技术，每天在影响着全球数十亿人的生活。它让企业更强大，让你的生活更美好，让未来的医疗更先进，让我们的地球更可持续。从这些维度上看，我们是非常幸运的一群人。所以我们要找到自己能做到最好的那件事——AMD选择的是高性能计算。我们不认为可以做所有事，但我们相信，在高性能计算这件事上，我们能为人类的生活带来真正美好的改变。这，就是我们的选择。 整理自 English / Passage12。本页于 2026-09-28 整理发布。

title: Why More Americans Are Unemployed For Longer
summary: 通过求职者的经历理解长期失业及其对家庭与生活的影响。
text: SummaryThis video examines long-term unemployment through job seekers’ experiences and economic commentary. It describes a low-hire, low-fire environment and explores how prolonged unemployment can affect income, confidence, health, families, and communities. The notes include idioms and a Chinese translation. Watch on YouTube Content 以下为原笔记中的视频转录与学习内容，保留原素材的叙述语境。 [数据引言] Over 1.8 million Americans have been classified as long-term unemployed in a given month in 2026, meaning they’ve been out of work for at least 27 weeks. That accounts for about a quarter of all unemployed Americans. Long-term unemployment has seen a sharp rise in the U.S., up about 55% from 2023 and 45% from 2019. [受访者个人陈述 ①] “I just recently got let go, or laid off, from a startup right before Thanksgiving. I thought that, you know, this was going to come around with your level of expertise and the amount of people that I’ve networked with my entire career — this is only going to be temporary. And I was shocked by the end of January that nothing had hit. I had refreshed my resume. I think I banged on every person’s door in my LinkedIn connections — I had found every single connection I had, and there was just cold lead after cold lead after cold lead, and a no. And so, ‘just give it a couple more weeks, this is going to work out.’ And then, you know, it really did — blink — and six months had flown by.” [经济学分析 ①] Economists are interested in this group of people because their experience can help determine the health of the American labor market. Think of it like this: if more Americans are taking months and months to find jobs, that can indicate the market has a higher barrier to entry and isn’t as strong. The rising amount of long-term unemployed people is a sign of the low-hire, low-fire environment, with companies reluctant to increase headcounts amid higher interest rates and the rise of artificial intelligence — it becomes more difficult, and can take longer, for people to find a job. That’s exemplified by the hiring rate for U.S. nonfarm payrolls, which stood at 3.5% in March. It’s trended downward since 2021, meaning companies have been adding workers at a slower rate. [受访者个人陈述 ②] “I’ve probably interviewed over 20 different times, and out of those 100 applications, I’ve probably been ghosted maybe 80 times. And so it’s not that we’re not trying — it’s the fact that we’re getting buried amongst each other, because there’s so many of us looking for jobs right now. There’s only so much that talent acquisition and HR departments can do to find the talent that their companies are looking for. We are quite literally all drowning in the unemployment crisis right now.” [经济学分析 ②] This kind of economy creates challenges, even for workers who already have jobs. With more people competing for fewer openings, employers have more leverage in today’s market. Year over year growth in wages has seen a significant drop from the highs of 2022. [长期失业的隐性代价] But just as costly is the hidden toll of long-term unemployment. First, there’s the personal costs that extend far beyond a single missed paycheck. Research shows that after a decade, long-term unemployed workers earned about 32% less than nondisplaced workers, compared with only 9% less for short-term unemployed workers. Job losses have also been linked to worsening mental and physical health, as well as greater social withdrawal. [专家评语] “What psychologists tell us is that, other than the death of a family member or a close friend, this is one of the most devastating things that people face. So it’s a very serious health problem and an economic problem.” [受访者个人陈述 ③] “The amount of rejection, the amount of ghosting eats away at you. Even with therapy, it’s still really hard to constantly be told that you’re not good enough or that there’s not a spot for you. And as someone that’s always carved their own way or found a path to success — it feels like there’s just a blockade in the road, and that no matter how big the bulldozer is that you’re pushing, or how hard you’re pushing yourself, that blockade is not moving.” [社会与宏观经济代价] Then there is the societal cost. Communities with high levels of long-term unemployment often see higher rates of crime and violence. Other studies have found that children who grow up with long-term parental unemployment tend to have significantly worse mental health in their adulthood. And lastly, it can hinder the growth of the U.S. economy. A widely adopted economic rule of thumb estimates that a one percentage point increase in the unemployment rate is associated with a 3% reduction in GDP. That’s because high unemployment often leads to the suppression of consumer spending, which accounts for almost 70% of America’s gross domestic product. [结语] For millions of Americans, long-term unemployment is more than a temporary setback. It can reshape their careers, families, and communities for years to come. Vocabulary & Expressions 原文表达 类型 说明 got let go / laid off 口语/委婉语 两者并列，前者更口语化，后者为正式说法，均指”被裁员” banged on every person’s door 习语 字面是”敲每扇门”，引申为”逐一联系、穷尽人脉” cold lead 行业术语 销售/求职语境中指”毫无回应的线索”，此处形容求职石沉大海 blink — six months had flown by 口语感叹 “一眨眼”六个月过去，强调时间流逝之快与落差之深 low-hire, low-fire environment 经济术语 “低招聘、低裁员”环境，指市场僵滞状态 ghosted 网络/口语 源自社交语境，指”对方突然消失、不回复”，此处用于求职被无视 getting buried amongst each other 比喻 求职者相互”掩埋”彼此，形容竞争激烈到简历淹没在人海中 drowning in the unemployment crisis 比喻 “溺于失业危机”，情绪强烈，有集体绝望感 eats away at you 习语 指负面情绪”侵蚀”心理，是英语中非常地道的表达 carved their own way 习语 “开辟自己的道路”，强调自力更生的个人性格 blockade in the road 比喻 道路上的”封锁线”，用于形容求职阻碍，后延伸出”推土机”意象，构成连贯隐喻 rule of thumb 习语 “经验法则”，指粗略但广泛认可的估算方式 nondisplaced workers 经济术语 指”未遭遇非自愿失业的工人”，对应”displaced workers（被迫失业者）” year over year 财经术语 “同比”，即与上一年同期相比 中文翻译 2026年，每个月有超过180万美国人被列为长期失业者，即已失业至少27周。这一群体约占全体失业人口的四分之一。美国长期失业人数正在急剧攀升——较2023年上涨约55%，较2019年上涨约45%。 [受访者] “感恩节前夕，我刚刚被那家初创公司裁了。我当时心想，凭我这些年积累的经验、凭我经营多年的人脉，这种事怎么可能长久——顶多是暂时的。结果到一月底，还是什么动静都没有，我真的惊了。简历早就更新了，LinkedIn上的人脉也几乎挨个儿敲了一遍，能找到的关系全都找了，换来的却是一个又一个冷回应，一个又一个拒绝。我只好安慰自己：’再等几个礼拜，肯定会有转机的。’然后——就这么一眨眼——六个月过去了。” 经济学家之所以关注这一群体，是因为他们的处境能够反映美国劳动力市场的健康状况。打个比方：如果越来越多的美国人要花上数月才能找到工作，这往往意味着市场的入门门槛在抬高，整体形势并不乐观。长期失业人数的上升，折射出当下”招人少、裁人也少”的市场僵局——在高利率环境与人工智能崛起的双重压力下，企业普遍不愿扩充人手，求职因此变得更难、也更耗时。这一点从美国非农就业的招聘率上便可见一斑：今年3月，该数据仅为3.5%，且自2021年以来持续走低，意味着企业增员的步伐越来越慢。 [受访者] “我大概面试了二十多次。在投出的一百份简历里，有八十份左右就那么石沉大海，对方根本没有任何回音。所以不是我们不努力——是因为我们彼此都在互相’掩埋’。现在找工作的人太多了，招聘和HR部门能做的毕竟有限。说真的，我们所有人，都正在被这场失业危机淹没。” 这样的经济环境，即便对已经在职的人也构成压力。竞争同一岗位的人越来越多，空缺却越来越少，雇主在谈判中占据了更强的主动权。工资的同比增幅，也已从2022年的高点显著回落。 而更沉重的，是长期失业背后那笔看不见的代价。首先是个人层面的代价，其冲击远不止于少拿几个月的薪水。研究表明，十年之后，长期失业者的收入仍比未经历失业的同龄人低约32%；而短期失业者，这一差距仅为9%。失业还与身心健康恶化、社会退缩等问题密切相关。 [专家] “心理学家告诉我们：除了至亲的离世，失业是人们所能面对的最具破坏性的人生事件之一。它既是一个严峻的健康问题，也是一个严峻的经济问题。” [受访者] “那种被拒绝的感觉，那种被无视的感觉，会一点一点地把你侵蚀掉。就算在接受心理咨询，也还是很难——一遍遍被人告知’你不够好’’没有你的位置’，这真的很难承受。我是那种一直靠自己闯出路来的人，但现在，感觉前面就是一道铁闸。不管你开的推土机有多大，不管你把自己逼得有多狠，那道闸就是纹丝不动。” 其次是社会层面的代价。 长期失业率高企的社区，往往伴随着更高的犯罪率和暴力事件。研究还发现，在父母长期失业的家庭中成长的孩子，成年后罹患心理健康问题的风险显著更高。最后，长期失业还会拖累整体经济增长。 一条被广泛认可的经济学经验法则指出：失业率每上升一个百分点，GDP将随之下降约3%。原因在于，高失业率往往压制居民消费，而消费支出约占美国国内生产总值的70%。 对数以百万计的美国人而言，长期失业绝非一次短暂的挫折。它可能在未来许多年里，重塑他们的职业轨迹、家庭结构，乃至整个社区的命运。 整理自 English / Passage11。本页于 2026-09-28 整理发布。

title: 12 Ways to Write Better Sentences for Creative Writers
summary: 学习让句子更清晰、更有节奏的十二种写作方法。
text: SummaryNovel editor Ellen Brock presents twelve ways to improve sentences in creative writing. The notes cover clarity, tone, active voice, filtering, pace, natural wording, and unnecessary words, with examples, writing terminology, and a Chinese translation. Watch on YouTube Content 以下为原笔记中的视频转录与学习内容，保留原素材的叙述语境。 Hey guys, it’s Ellen Brock, novel editor. I hope you’re all doing really, really well today. Today we’re going to talk about 12 ways to write better sentences as a creative writer. I’m also working on a video of ways to write better paragraphs that will probably come out in the new year, so stay tuned for that if you think that would help you. Today, my goal with this video is to really help your writing to sound more professional—more like a published author. There are some tips and tricks that can really help to give your writing that extra edge, that extra sense of professionalism, which will be really helpful when you go to query publishers or agents, or wherever you’re trying to get your story seen. There may always be reasons why, for you in particular, you might want to ignore a tip that I give in this video, and that’s completely fine. There are a wide variety of writing styles, and sometimes you might go against a certain tip because you want to create a certain effect, and that’s totally fine. But for the most part, my tips in this video should apply no matter what point of view, style, or genre you’re writing in. These are really just ways to give your writing a little bit of a professional polish. So with that said, let’s go ahead and get right into the tips. Number 1: Avoid confusingly complex sentences.Longer, more complicated sentences might be something that you do choose to do for a stylistic effect. It might also be something that you want to use to break up monotony, so you want to make your sentences have different lengths and structures so that it doesn’t become repetitive or monotonous in sound. However, when you use overly complicated sentences unnecessarily or too often, it actually slows down the reading process because the reader has to try a lot harder to understand the meaning of that sentence—what you’re trying to say, how it’s relevant—and that can make the writing itself feel too slow. It can also make the actions feel more distant because you start to layer concepts and cram concepts into the same sentence. I’m going to give an example to hopefully clarify what I mean: “Because Jessica was hungry due to missing breakfast, which happened because Jake, her brother, had taken too long to get ready in their shared bedroom, she was forced to once again circle around the large block looking for the food truck that always seemed to be in a different place each day.” This sentence is grammatically correct. It’s pretty understandable in isolation and doesn’t really pose any particular problem. But if you were to take a sentence like this and combine it with several other lengthy, complicated sentences—either right up against each other or even just many times on a page or in a chapter—it will really slow down the process of reading. The reader will have to spend longer understanding what you’re saying, it may bury the point you’re trying to make, and it may also create distance from the action. So normally, complicated sentences like this are better off broken up into smaller sentences. For example, we could rewrite this sentence: “Jessica’s stomach rumbled. If Jake hadn’t taken so long to get ready in their shared bathroom, she would have had time to eat breakfast. Her heels clacked against the sidewalk as she walked around the block looking for the food truck. Why did they park the thing in a different place every day?” Notice how breaking up this sentence, as a bonus, also gives us more room for sensory details, for some personality and introspection, and it really helps to create a more immersive experience for the reader. If you have trouble identifying when sentences are getting kind of complicated or lengthy, someone on my Discord recommended the Hemingway Editor. If you put this sentence into the Hemingway Editor, it has no problem identifying that the original version is very hard to read and that the edited version is easy to read. So that’s something that you could use if you do struggle to tell when a sentence is getting too complicated. The Hemingway Editor actually can help with several of the things that we’re going to talk about in this video, so that’s just a little tip that might help you. Number 2: Set the tone with word choices.Often when we’re writing, we can choose from a variety of words that mean basically the same thing as what we’re trying to say, but different words have very different connotations and evoke different kinds of moods. By choosing the right word, you can really improve the overall tone and vibe of your writing. For example: “The boat sliced through the water” feels aggressive or strong. “The boat bobbed across the water” feels lazy or slow. “The boat floated over the water” might feel hopeful or even uplifting. This also goes for similes. If you’re writing a romantic scene, you don’t want to describe the roses like blood spots on the bed. And if you’re writing a horror, you don’t want to describe the long hallway as a giraffe’s neck because it just doesn’t set the right mood and tone. So be thoughtful about the words that you’re choosing and the impact that’s having on the vibe that your writing is creating. Let’s look at an example from the novel The Ritual by Adam Nevill. This is, of course, a horror novel, and pay attention to the words that he chooses: “He was interrupted by a crash out there somewhere in the length and breadth of the countless trees, in the ocean of invisible ruin and tangle. A great bough or strong limb had been snapped in half. The sounds of its breaking seemed to shoot in so many directions it became impossible to guess where the sound originated.” Notice how the word choices emphasize the largeness of the woods with “the ocean of invisible ruin and tangle.” Also notice the emphasis on more aggressive-sounding words like “snapped in half” rather than “broke,” and the sound “shoots” in so many directions rather than “bounces” or “echoes.” Try to create the mood or the vibe that you want the reader to experience with your word choices, and this will really go a long way towards improving your writing. Number 3: Avoid passive voice.You’ve probably heard a million times that you should avoid passive voice. Sometimes it can be a little tricky to understand what that means, but to make it as simple as possible: passive voice is when the subject of a sentence or the clause of a sentence receives the action instead of performs the action. So if you’re struggling to tell if it is passive voice or not, just try to ask yourself: “Is the subject doing the action? Are they performing the action?” For example, “The door was held by Henry” is passive because the door is not doing the action, whereas “Henry held the door” is active. Henry is the one doing the action of holding the door. Often in fiction, this can be a problem because it results in de-emphasizing the character doing the action. Here’s another example: “Megan was chased by Elizabeth” is weak compared to “Elizabeth chased Megan.” In the first sentence, Megan is receiving the action, and then at the end… in the second sentence, Elizabeth is doing the action. Even if Megan is the protagonist (the character we generally want to emphasize more), the writing will feel stronger if we focus on the person doing the action. If we do want to put more emphasis on Megan, another option might be “Megan ran from Elizabeth,” which puts the emphasis on Megan and allows Megan to still be the one who’s actually doing the action—so we’re still not using passive voice. There may, of course, be situations where we want to use passive voice on purpose to create a certain effect, such as intentionally creating distance. A character might do this for some reason, such as not wanting to take responsibility or maybe feeling guilty. So in deep third-person POV or in first-person POV, it’s possible that passive voice might help to convey that intentional distancing from the action, but I would say that that type of situation is relatively rare. If you do need help identifying passive voice, again, the Hemingway Editor can really help with that; it does a pretty good job of identifying passive voice. Number 4: Remove filtering.So, filtering is when the experience of the story is filtered through the POV (point of view) character, so that character’s experience is emphasized as separate from the reader. That’s not really what the intention is; that’s just the effect of filtering. Filtering typically involves using words like thought, knew, felt, saw, smelled, tasted—things that create a separation from the sensory experience and the reader. I’m going to give examples because I think that makes this a lot easier to understand. A common filtering word in amateur fiction is saw. For example: “Rebecca saw the tail of a fox sticking out from the brush.” It’s more distancing than “The tail of a fox stuck out from the brush.” Of course, there are sensory words where there isn’t really any way to work around them, for example, smelled and tasted. It’s not really easy or feasible to try to write a sentence where you describe that without using the word smelled or tasted, but we can still create a slightly more immersive effect by, again, eliminating filtering that through the point of view character. For example: “Inside the house, Jake smelled green tea and baked bread” could be easily made stronger by rewriting it as “The house smelled of green tea and baked bread,” which eliminates that distance between the sensory experience and the reader. Introspection can also be less impactful and more distancing when we use filtering like knew, wondered, thought, and things along those lines. Whenever we’re using a deep point of view or first-person point of view, we can assume that it’s the character (the POV character) thinking the thought or having the realization. So those words just add a little bit of extra and unnecessary separation between the reader and that thought or realization. For example: “James thought it was impossible that Katie didn’t know that already” is a lot weaker than “It was impossible for Katie not to know that already.” We don’t need to say that James thought it was impossible because James is the point of view character, so we can simply say “It was impossible,” and it doesn’t make the writing feel quite as distant. Of course, there are times where filtering might help with clarity, such as an omniscient point of view where there’s a difference between what the narrator knows and experiences versus what the characters know and experience. So in that case, filtering might help with clarity. But for most writers today, the majority are writing in deep third limited or first person, and in neither of those cases is filtering really beneficial. Let’s look at an example from The Ritual. At the beginning of this excerpt, it’s pointed out that a character is watching something, which is a form of filtering. However, in this case, the character is exhausted and inactive, so it may be intended to put emphasis on this inaction by saying that he watched what’s occurring. But note how the rest of the paragraph has no filtering and a lot of sensory details: “Luke watched. He pushed the last leg of the stool through the door of the iron stove they were huddled around. A shower of sparks erupted inside as he rooted the ancient wooden spoke around the hearth. They coughed in the acrid smoke that belched out; the chimney was almost totally closed. Smoldering remnants of the seat formed the base to the red ashes inside the little oven that only heated part of the ground floor before the drafts from the door and between the floorboards took over with a night chill, a tang of damp earth, and the ferment of rotten wood.” In that excerpt, we get a lot of sensory information—sights and smells, even a little bit of taste maybe, of the smoke—and we did not need to use filtering words to bring that across, so it’s a much more immersive experience for the reader. So if possible, eliminating filtering is a great way to make the reading experience feel a lot more immediate, a lot more connected to the reader. Number 5: Set the pace with sentence length.It’s not only word choices that can help with setting the tone or the mood; the sentence length can also go a long way towards setting the tone or mood of a scene. For example, in most cases, if the character is being thoughtful or maybe they’re distant from something that occurred, longer sentences tend to work better. They give a more introspective, thoughtful mood. Whereas if the character is involved in an intense or immediate emotional situation—action, urgency, all of that—it is better conveyed by shorter, choppier sentences. This is a really great way to control the pace that the reader reads. When we have shorter, choppier sentences, we tend to read faster, and that can help to give a sense of tension and urgency. Whereas when you want to give that more creative, thoughtful, introspective type of vibe—maybe the character is observing things, they’re thinking about the way things look—the descriptions (visual descriptions, sensory descriptions), those things tend to work better in longer form with longer sentences. Slower reading time equals more of an experiential vibe. Let’s look at two examples from the same book. We’re going to look at We Need to Talk About Kevin by Lionel Shriver. Notice in this intense scene, where the protagonist comes home to a concerningly quiet house, how short the sentences are: “As I advanced down the hall, I paused at Celia’s bedroom and had to force myself to walk in. It was dark. Her bed was empty. The same in the master bedroom. The bathrooms. Out on the deck. Nothing. Nobody. Where were you? Had you gone looking for me? I had a mobile; you knew the number. And why wouldn’t you have taken the truck? Was this a game? Were you hiding, giggling in a closet with Celia? This, of all nights, you chose to play a game?” The shortness conveys her sense of panic and urgency. We can compare this to another point in the book that focuses more on reflection or thoughtfulness: “Before you condemn me utterly, I beg you to understand just how hard I’d been trying to be a good mother. But trying to be a good mother may be as distant from being a good mother as trying to have a good time is from truly having one. Distrusting my every impulse from the instant he was laid on my breast, I’d followed a devout regime of hugging my little boy an average of three times a day, admiring something he did or said at least twice, and reciting ‘I love you, kiddo’ or ‘You know that your daddy and I love you very much’ with the predictable uniformity of liturgical professions of faith.” The longer sentences here convey a sense of thoughtfulness as well as emotional distance from the material being discussed. She’s explaining here and wants to be understood, but there isn’t an urgency, and the emotions of the situation feel at least partly past. But if the sentences were shorter or choppier, it would instead come across as more desperate or panicked, or maybe that she has an immense stake in being understood in this exact moment. The sentence length can vary a lot throughout the novel, even throughout individual scenes. It’s a great way to control the pacing, and it can really give your writing that extra edge. Number 6: Avoid body parts taking action.This is a very common habit that amateur writers can get into, but it’s very easy to fix. So once you’re aware of it, you can easily cut it out of your writing. Sometimes the way sentences are written, the body part of a character is given the action rather than the character themselves doing the action. For example: “His foot kicked the ball” gives the action to the foot, while “He kicked the ball” gives the action to the person. “Her hand grabbed the pen” gives the action to her hand, while “She grabbed the pen” gives the action to the person. This again creates unnecessary distance from the action, but it’s very simple and easy to take out of your writing. It’s definitely something I recommend to give your writing a little more strength. Number 7: Reduce “was -ing” construction.This is another super easy one once you’re aware, and you can easily remove it from your writing. That is just the “was -ing” construction. Was running, was dancing, was jumping feels more distant from the reader and also just feels weaker. For example: “He was running down the street” could be easily made stronger by rewriting it as “He ran down the street.” “She was jumping up and down” is better as “She jumped up and down.” “He was sitting on the couch thinking about what he would do” is not as strong as “He sat on the couch and thought about what he would do.” Of course, there might be situations where the “was -ing” construction just sounds more natural or does convey a slightly different meaning, and in that case, it’s completely fine. We should always go with what sounds best and most natural. For example, in dialogue, if a character asks another character, “Where were you at 3 p.m. yesterday?” they will most likely respond with, “I was driving home from work,” rather than, “At 3 p.m. yesterday, I drove home from work.” With all of these tips, the point is to make the writing feel stronger, so if one of these tips ever makes your writing feel more unnatural or awkward, of course, don’t follow it. Number 8: Keep the wording natural.Often, writers might go for more unnatural phrasing in an attempt to sound more sophisticated, old-fashioned, or “writerly.” But normally, this doesn’t enhance the writing; it can feel a little bit awkward or even maybe stiff. For example: “He placed the book upon the dresser” rather than “He set the book on the dresser.” The second sentence is a lot more natural, a lot more how modern people would talk or explain something. The more sophisticated, old-fashioned “He placed the book upon the dresser” sounds kind of awkward to modern readers. Sometimes this could also take the form of avoiding contractions, such as writing, “He did not know what he should do” rather than “He didn’t know what to do.” There might, of course, be situations where it makes sense for the personality of your character, or maybe the narrator, or the style of writing—there may be reasons why going for a more old-fashioned or sophisticated sound makes sense or works for you. But for the majority of writers, this is just going to seem odd and unnatural, and it’s going to create distance because of that unnatural sound. That’s going to make it seem less immediate, less close to the reader. So for most people, it is better to just use the more natural-sounding sentence rather than trying to sound sophisticated or writerly. Sometimes this can happen because writers read older books more often, so that’s what books sound like to them. It might also happen if you come from an academic writing background or a scientific writing background. Number 9: Cut unnecessary similes.So, similes (or comparisons using like or as) do have a place in writing. I don’t want to suggest that you cannot use them at all; they actually can be used very effectively. But often, amateur writers or new writers might use similes excessively, or in situations where a simile just doesn’t add anything or doesn’t make sense. Normally, similes for common or well-understood concepts, descriptions, and things like that just don’t really serve any purpose. For example: “He stomped the snow off his shoes like a drummer beating a drum.” This doesn’t really offer any meaningful additional information because we all know what it sounds like and looks like to stomp snow from our shoes. Additionally, similes don’t work well when the comparison is too similar to the original thing. With a simile, we’re trying to add to or enhance the reader’s understanding of the description. For example: “He ran across the yard like a soccer player running for the ball.” This doesn’t really add new information because it’s just a different way to say that the character is running. We’re not looking to just say the same thing in a different way. Similes should seek to enhance the reader’s understanding of something that might be unfamiliar or something difficult to grasp, or it should try to set the mood or the tone in a way that might not be obvious inherently with just a simple description. For example, let’s look at this simile from The Handmaid’s Tale by Margaret Atwood: “The tulips are red, a darker crimson towards the stem, as if they have been cut and are beginning to heal there.” This creates a clearly dark tone, whereas just describing the tulips on their own as darker right at the stem doesn’t have any particular connotation when it comes to mood, tone, or vibe. Here’s another example: “Without his uniform he looks smaller, older, like something being dried.” This makes the character being described feel clearly unappealing, which adds a layer of additional meaning. Let’s look at one last example from The Ritual: “Then he realized he could feel nothing, nothing at all, as if every nerve had been stripped from out of his body, like wiring torn from a wall cavity.” The simile emphasizes the horror element and makes the character’s experience more evocative and more visceral. Similes can be a great way to enhance the mood or tone, or to help the reader grasp something that’s difficult to understand. Just make sure that you’re not including similes just for the heck of it when they’re not really contributing anything to the novel. Number 10: Use vocabulary level strategically.Vocabulary level can be a great way to convey characterization, values, education level, and all sorts of different things, but that’s not really what I want to talk about in this video. What I want you to focus on with vocabulary level is the effect that it has on reading speed. When you use more advanced vocabulary—bigger words, even if you use bigger words that are fairly common and not super obscure—it really slows down the reader. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing; it’s just something to be aware of. Some books are meant to be read more slowly. Some genres, some target reader groups like to read things slowly, whereas other groups prefer something faster-paced. Other genres do better with a faster, more clipped pacing, which can be better achieved with a lower vocabulary level. So pay attention to how your word choices, in terms of the complexity of the words and the advancedness of the words, can impact how slowly or quickly the reader gets through the text. Let’s look at an example from We Need to Talk About Kevin. This is a good example of more advanced vocabulary being used to convey character in a novel, but also, in my opinion, this book is best read slowly, and the more advanced vocabulary helps to slow the reader down and really experience the story alongside the protagonist. In this excerpt, the protagonist is describing the difference between her troubled son Kevin’s and her daughter Celia’s infancies: “Kevin’s disconsolate infancy had segued to wholesale boredom. Celia was entranced by the least bauble, every bit as delighted with a scrap of colored tissue paper as with that expensive mother-of-pearl mobile over her crib. She displayed an indiscriminate fascination with a tactile universe that would have driven your Madison Avenue masters to distraction.” We can compare this to a book that, again in my opinion, is a bit of a quicker read, yet with no less personality or characterization in the writing. This is an excerpt from Survivor by Chuck Palahniuk. From this example, we can really tell that a simpler vocabulary level doesn’t mean that you can’t make interesting points or have a unique style: “Next to the speakerphone is a fat daily planner book they keep full of things for me to get done. They want me to account for the next ten years, task by task, their way. Everything in your life turns into an item on a list, something to accomplish. You get to see how your life looks flattened out. The shortest distance between two points is a timeline, a schedule, a map of your time, the itinerary for the rest of your life. Nothing shows you the straight line from here to death like a list.” The excerpt from Survivor is written at a third-grade reading level, and the excerpt from We Need to Talk About Kevin is written at a ninth-grade reading level. This is a really big difference in reading level, but both books feel mature, they both feel interesting, and they both have a lot of characterization. So there’s no sense that it’s less sophisticated to write at a lower reading level. What it does do is it makes the book read a lot faster. I think, for me, I read Survivor in probably two or three days, whereas I read We Need to Talk About Kevin over probably a month or a month and a half.
